prompt:
9B. European Union Policy
Examine the impact of European Union policy on the development of primary economic activity in Ireland.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Impact 1: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) modernised Irish farming.
Ireland joined the EEC in 1973 and applied the CAP straight away. Irish farming changed from small subsistence family farms to a specialised, market-centred industry.
Guaranteed minimum prices for milk, beef and cereals gave farmers a secure income. The Headage Payment Scheme (1975) paid farmers per animal, so cattle and sheep numbers and milk production rose sharply.
Grants for modernisation led to fewer, larger, specialised dairy and beef farms focused on exports.
Milk quotas (1984) limited production to cut surpluses. When they were abolished in 2015, over 18,000 farmers spent EUR 1.4 billion expanding herds. Output per dairy farm rose from 70,000 litres in 1984 to 585,000 litres in 2024.
Decoupling in 2003 paid farmers by farm size, not by number of animals. This gave small farmers a stable income without pressure to intensify.
Not all impacts were positive. EU sugar reforms in 2006 cut the guaranteed sugar price by 36%, affecting over 3,700 sugar beet growers and closing the Carlow and Mallow plants.
Today schemes such as ACRES pay farmers to protect biodiversity and water quality.

Impact 2: The Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) changed Irish fishing.
Ireland had to share its waters. Foreign trawlers overfished, and herring and cod were almost wiped out in the late 1970s. In 2024, 36% of fish landings in Ireland were by foreign trawlers.
Total Allowable Catch quotas, bigger mesh sizes and the Irish Conservation Box protect stocks, but Ireland gets only a small share of the catch from its own waters.
Decommissioning schemes cut fleets and jobs on the Western Seaboard.
On the positive side, EU funds modernised harbours at Killybegs and Baltimore, and exports grew to EUR 1.24 billion in 2024.
marking_scheme: Impact on primary activity identified 2 marks. Examination 14 x SRPs (2 marks each). A 2nd impact identified is credited 1 x SRP. Reference to a policy is credited 1 x SRP. All further impacts and policies need examination. Examination with no reference to the impact of EU policy on primary activity: max 2 x SRPs. Examination with no reference to EU policy: max 2 x SRPs. Positive and negative viewpoints accepted.
source: 2021 State Exam - Part Two Section 3, Q9 B

prompt:
9C. Conflict of Interest
Examine how conflict may arise between the exploitation of natural resources and the need to protect the environment, with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Example 1: Fishing in Irish waters.
Ireland's seas are rich in fish because of the warm, unpolluted water and a long continental shelf full of plankton. Fishing is important for jobs in coastal communities.
After Ireland joined the EEC in 1973, foreign trawlers with modern technology fished in Irish waters. Herring and cod were overfished and almost wiped out in the late 1970s.
To protect fish stocks, the EU's Common Fisheries Policy set Total Allowable Catch quotas, limited seasons and days at sea, and banned the fishing of endangered species. The minimum mesh size was raised to 100 mm so young fish could escape.
This caused conflict with fishers. Quotas cut catches and incomes, and decommissioning schemes caused job losses on the Western Seaboard. Many Irish fishers feel the quota system is unfair.
Aquaculture also causes conflict: salmon farms bring jobs, but sea lice, disease and escaped farmed fish threaten wild fish.

Example 2: Intensive dairy farming.
When EU milk quotas ended in 2015, farmers expanded their herds to exploit grass and land. Irish dairying became the fastest-growing dairy market in the EU.
But intensive dairy and beef farming release methane from livestock and nitrous oxide from fertilisers. Agriculture makes up more than 40% of Ireland's emissions.
Runoff of nitrates and phosphates from slurry and fertilisers pollutes streams, rivers and lakes.
This creates a conflict between farm incomes and protecting the environment. Food Vision 2030 tries to balance both, with ideas such as reducing herd sizes, rewetting land and planting legumes that need no fertiliser.

source: 2021 State Exam - Part Two Section 3, Q9 C

prompt:
10B. Dynamics of Population
Examine how changing fertility and mortality rates impact on population structure with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Examples: Ireland and India.

Falling fertility narrows the base of the population pyramid.
In Ireland in 1961 the total fertility rate (TFR) was 3.78 and families had over four children. By 2024 it had fallen to 1.5, below the replacement level of 2.1.
Reasons include women staying in education and work, later motherhood (first-time mothers averaged 31.7 years in 2024), contraception and high housing and childcare costs.
As a result, fewer children are born and the base of Ireland's pyramid has become narrower. Children aged 0-14 are now about 18% of the population, smaller than in earlier decades.
In India the TFR fell from about 6.1 in the 1950s to about 2.1 today. India still has an expansive pyramid with a wide base (about 24% under 15), but the base is slowly narrowing.

Falling mortality widens the top of the pyramid.
In Ireland, better healthcare, living standards and diet have raised life expectancy to about 83. Death rates are low, so the sides of the pyramid are almost straight and the top is wider.
People aged 65+ were 15.7% of the population in 2022 and could reach 30% by 2050. Ireland is in Stage 4 of the Demographic Transition Model with low birth and death rates.
This raises the dependency ratio, now about 52 dependants per 100 workers, putting pressure on pensions and healthcare.
In India, death rates fell while birth rates stayed high (Stage 3), so the population grew rapidly. Life expectancy is about 70 and only 7-8% are over 65, but the top will widen as more people survive into old age.
marking_scheme: Impact of changing fertility rates identified 2 marks. Impact of changing mortality rates identified 2 marks. Example of where impacts occur 2 marks. Examination 12 x SRPs (2 marks each). Emphasis is on the impact of changing fertility and mortality rates. No reference to impact on population structure: max 2 x SRPs. Max 6 x SRPs if only changing fertility OR only changing mortality examined. Max 2 x SRPs if the answer does not deal with 'changing' rates.
source: 2021 State Exam - Part Two Section 3, Q10 B

prompt:
10C. Migration
With reference to a developed region that you have studied, explain the impact of migration on each of the following:
- Rural areas
- Urban areas.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Developed region: Ireland.

Rural areas - impact: rural depopulation and decline.
Young people leave rural areas for jobs, colleges and services in towns and cities. This leaves smaller, older communities, especially in the remote west and north-west, e.g. Mayo, Donegal and Connemara.
With fewer young people, schools, shops, post offices and pubs close. Moygownagh, Co. Mayo has lost 90% of its population since 1841 and lost its shop, pub and post office.
Older people left behind can become lonely and isolated, and sports clubs lose members.
Gaeltacht areas such as Connemara and Ballyferriter declined as young people left to find work.
However, some rural areas near cities gain people. Remote workers and commuters move out for cheaper housing, e.g. Allenwood, Co. Kildare grew by 494% between 1996 and 2022, and Gorey, Co. Wexford grew by 26.4% (2011-2022). These areas may then lack school places, public transport and healthcare.

Urban areas - impact: growth, diversity and pressure on services (Dublin).
Migrants fill labour gaps in Dublin's hospitals, tech firms, hotels and construction. In 2024 Ireland had a net migration gain of 79,300.
Dublin is the most culturally diverse region: over 17% of residents are non-Irish, with large communities from Brazil, India, Romania, Poland and Nigeria. This brings new shops, languages and festivals.
But demand for housing is at an all-time high, with the highest rents and house prices in Ireland and a higher risk of homelessness.
Schools need English as an Additional Language classes, and hospitals and GPs are under pressure.
Some tension has arisen, e.g. the 2024 Dublin riots, linked to fears about the pace of immigration.

Not tied to Ireland. Impacts may be positive or negative; can be inward migration, outward migration or both. Do not accept a developing region. Max 6 x SRPs if only rural or only urban impact explained.

prompt:
15. Views of development and underdevelopment are subject to change.
Discuss.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Development used to be seen simply as making money. Over time, views have changed to include people's wellbeing, fairness and the environment.

Aspect 1: Development measured by wealth (GDP and GNI).
For a long time a country was judged 'developed' by how much it earned. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year. GDP per capita divides this by the population.
GDP is easy to compare because every country calculates it the same way, and rising GDP usually means more jobs and profits.
But this view has weaknesses. GDP shows total money, not who has it, so it can rise when only a few wealthy people earn more. It ignores health, wellbeing, pollution and unpaid work such as caring for family.
It also leaves out the informal economy, such as street vendors in Nigeria. In sub-Saharan Africa over 85% of jobs are informal, so GDP and GNI make these countries look poorer than they really are.

Aspect 2: Modernisation - copying the rich countries.
Modernisation theory says that poorer countries will become wealthy if they copy richer ones by investing in modern technology, industry and education. Development happens in stages: traditional farming societies become urban, industrial ones.
China followed this path, moving from a rural, farming country to a world leader in technology and industry. Millions moved to cities such as Shenzhen, and many people were lifted out of poverty.
But views of this approach have changed. It caused inequality between rich cities and poor rural areas, and environmental damage. In Beijing, cars rose from 77,000 in 1978 to millions by 2018. Critics say every country is unique, so one model does not suit all.

Aspect 3: Protectionism.
Some governments believe development comes from protecting home industries with tariffs, quotas and subsidies. The US put tariffs on steel imports to help its steel industry.
This protects jobs in the short term, but consumers pay higher prices, and other countries often retaliate, starting trade wars. So this view is also disputed.

Aspect 4: Sustainable and human development.
Today development is increasingly seen as improving quality of life without harming future generations. Sustainable development has three pillars: environmental, economic and social.
The UN's Human Development Index (HDI) measures life expectancy, education and income, not just wealth. Ireland scores 0.949 while Afghanistan scores only 0.462. The Gender Development Index compares the opportunities of men and women.
The Sustainable Development Goals include ending poverty, fighting climate change and providing clean water for everyone. Finland ranked first on the 2025 SDG Index by balancing growth with recycling, clean transport, health and education.

Conclusion: views of development have changed from a narrow focus on money to a wider view that includes health, education, equality and the environment. No single measure is perfect, so several are used together.

prompt:
16. Various soil patterns have developed because of the action of different soil forming processes.
Discuss.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Ireland has four main soil types: brown earths, gleys, podzols and peat. Each develops where a different soil-forming process is most active, giving a clear pattern of soils across the country.

Aspect 1: Humification - brown earth soils in the south and east.
Humification is the breakdown of dead leaves and plant litter into humus, a dark, jelly-like substance. In the south and east, lower rainfall (about 800 mm a year in Dublin) and slightly warmer, brighter weather let earthworms, fungi and bacteria stay active for most of the year, as the ground rarely freezes.
They decompose plant litter quickly, so the soil is rich in humus and dark in colour. Worms mix the organic and mineral matter, so there are no sharp layers.
Brown earths formed on glacial deposits under the deciduous oak and ash forests that once covered the east and south. They have a loamy texture and a crumbly, granular structure, so they are well drained and well aerated.
This makes them the most common soil in Ireland and the best for arable farming, e.g. in Co. Wexford and Co. Meath.

Aspect 2: Leaching and podzolisation - podzol soils.
Leaching happens when heavy rain washes nutrients down from the topsoil into lower horizons.
Podzols form in areas of heavy rainfall, often under coniferous forest, e.g. parts of Co. Cork and Co. Cavan. Pine needles give poor, acidic litter, so there is little microbial activity and a raw, acid humus forms on top.
Continuous leaching removes minerals from the upper soil, leaving an ash-grey layer. Iron and organic matter build up lower down and form a hard iron pan.
The iron pan stops water draining, so the soil above becomes waterlogged. Podzols are infertile, e.g. hard pans around Ballyhaunis, Co. Mayo cause poor drainage and low yields.

Aspect 3: Gleying - gley soils.
Gley soils form where rainfall is high and drainage is poor, such as on low-lying plains or over impermeable bedrock with a lot of clay, e.g. Cavan, Monaghan, Leitrim and Clare.
The soil is waterlogged, so micro-organisms use up all the oxygen while decomposing organic matter. This is called anaerobic reduction.
Chemical reactions then turn the iron a bluish-grey colour, which is leached down the profile, giving waterlogged blue-grey clay.
Poor aeration and constant waterlogging give a blocky structure that restricts roots, so gleys are only moderately fertile.

Aspect 4: Waterlogging and peat formation.
Peat soils form in the midlands and west, where heavy rain, poor drainage and long-term waterlogging occur. The lack of oxygen and acidic conditions stop microbes decomposing plant litter.
Wetland plants such as sphagnum moss build up faster than they decay, forming dark peat that is over 90% water. Ireland has 8% of the world's blanket bogs, which store millions of tonnes of carbon.

Conclusion: different processes - humification, leaching, gleying and waterlogging - act in different places, depending on rainfall, drainage and vegetation, and so produce Ireland's distinct pattern of soils.

prompt:
17. Discuss how soil development is influenced by any three of the following factors:
- Mineral matter
- Air
- Water
- Organic matter.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1: Mineral matter.
Mineral matter comes from the weathering of rock (the parent material) and from deposits such as glacial till.
Brown earth soils in Ireland developed on glacial deposits about 10,000 years old. These contain a variety of minerals and give a loamy texture - a balance of sand, silt and clay. This gives the soil a granular structure that drains well and lets air in.
The type of rock affects the soil. In west Galway, granite weathers into poor clay soils that are unsuitable for tillage. Where the bedrock is impermeable and has a high clay content, water cannot drain away and gley soils form, e.g. in Cavan and Leitrim.
Where rainfall is heavy, minerals are washed down the profile. In podzols, iron builds up lower down to form a hard iron pan.
Mineral matter also affects pH. Brown earths range from slightly alkaline to slightly acidic, depending on the parent material, which suits micro-organisms.

Aspect 2: Water.
The amount of rain and how well it drains strongly affect how soils develop.
Ireland's west receives about 1,600 mm of rain a year because of relief rainfall, almost twice as much as the east (about 800 mm), which lies in the rain shadow.
Heavy rain causes leaching: nutrients are washed down out of the topsoil. In wet areas under coniferous forest, this forms infertile, acidic podzols with a grey leached layer and an iron pan.
Where water cannot drain, the soil becomes waterlogged. In gley soils, the iron turns blue-grey and the soil gets a blocky structure that restricts roots.
In the wettest, worst-drained places, permanent waterlogging forms peat, which is over 90% water.
In the drier east there is little leaching, so brown earths are well drained. Because they hold humus, they do not waterlog in heavy rain or dry out in dry spells.

Aspect 3: Organic matter.
Organic matter is dead plant and animal material such as fallen leaves. When it decays it forms humus, which gives soil a dark colour and adds nutrients.
In the mild Irish climate, earthworms, insects, fungi and bacteria break down litter for most of the year. Under the oak and ash forests of the east and south, leaves decayed rapidly and formed fertile brown earths with a mild humus.
Badgers digging setts and worms mixing the soil spread organic matter through the profile, so there are no sharp layers.
Where litter is poor, such as pine needles under conifers, decay is slow and a raw, acid humus (mor) forms, as in podzols.
In waterlogged bogs there is little oxygen, so microbes cannot break down the plant matter. Sphagnum moss builds up faster than it decays and forms peat.

Air also matters: well-aerated soils, such as brown earths, let microbes work, while waterlogged soils lose their oxygen (anaerobic reduction).

Conclusion: the balance of mineral matter, water and organic matter decides whether a fertile brown earth or an infertile podzol, gley or peat develops.

prompt:
19. Examine how conflict can arise between political structures and cultural groups.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Political structures are things like states, borders and governments. Cultural groups share a religion, language or ethnic identity. When borders and governments do not match where cultural groups live, conflict can follow.

Aspect 1: Borders drawn along religious lines - the Partition of India.
In 1947 Britain granted independence to British India and divided it along religious and cultural lines into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan (West Pakistan and East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh in 1971).
The new borders left Muslim minorities in India and Hindu minorities in Pakistan. This led to riots.
About 12 million people fled Pakistan for India and over 10 million went the other way. About 1 million died in violent clashes, creating lasting bitterness between the two states.

Aspect 2: A disputed territory - Kashmir.
Kashmir is a mountainous region of 15 million people. In 1947 its ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, decided to join India, even though 80% of the people were Muslims who wanted to join Pakistan. War broke out.
The UN brought an uneasy peace in 1948, and a ceasefire line, the Line of Control, was agreed in 1949. Western Kashmir went to Pakistan and the east stayed under Indian control.
There is still no lasting peace. Indian Kashmir has a Muslim majority (60%) that wants to join Pakistan. Wars broke out in 1965 and 1999.
In 2019 India split the region into two union territories, which aimed to increase Hindu control. This caused outrage in Kashmir and Pakistan.
In 2025 militants killed 26 people in Pahalgam. India launched strikes on Pakistan and both sides came close to war. Both are nuclear powers, so the world fears a wider war. Kashmiris suffer from repression, collapsed tourism and damaged services.

Aspect 3: Separatist movements in north-east India.
A separatist movement is a group trying to break away and form its own state, often because of differences in ethnicity, culture or religion.
In north-east India, ethnic violence and separatist movements have caused conflict with the state. In Manipur in 2024, 70 people were killed and 60,000 left the region, many to refugee camps or Delhi.

Aspect 4: Northern Ireland and migrants in the EU.
In Northern Ireland, the Troubles were a conflict between communities with different political and cultural identities. Catholic nationalist communities suffered higher unemployment and lower wages. The Good Friday Agreement (1998) brought peace, and living standards gradually improved.
Today in the EU, far-right parties such as the National Rally in France and the AfD in Germany blame immigrants for social problems. This creates conflict between some governments and migrant cultural groups, and threatens values like equality and human rights.

Conclusion: conflict arises when political borders and governments ignore the wishes of cultural groups. It can lead to war, displacement and lasting division, as in India, Pakistan and Kashmir.

prompt:
22. Examine the uneven distribution of temperature over the earth's surface.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Temperatures vary greatly over the Earth, from about 27 degrees C all year near the equator to below -50 degrees C in polar winters. Several factors cause this.

Aspect 1: Latitude and the curvature of the Earth.
Because the Earth is curved, the sun heats it unequally.
At the equator, the sun's rays strike almost directly. They are concentrated on a small area and pass through a small amount of atmosphere, so little energy is lost. Tropical areas average about 27 degrees C with a narrow range of 24-30 degrees C.
Towards the poles, the rays come in at a low angle. They spread over a much larger area and pass through more atmosphere, so they give much less heat. Polar summers average only 0 degrees C, so snow and ice stay all year.
The Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5 degrees, so temperatures also change with the seasons. In summer a hemisphere is tilted towards the sun, so rays are more direct and days are longer. In winter it is tilted away and rays are spread out.
Albedo adds to the difference. Snow and ice reflect up to 90% of the sun's radiation, so polar regions stay cold.

Aspect 2: Ocean currents and prevailing winds.
Warm currents flow away from the equator and warm the air above them. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry warm tropical water towards Ireland and north-west Europe, keeping winters mild and coasts ice-free.
Cold currents flow from the poles towards the equator and cool the air, e.g. the Labrador Current near Greenland and the Canaries Current off west Africa.
Prevailing winds carry this heat onto land. Ireland's south-westerly winds bring warm air from near the tropics. Newfoundland, at a similar latitude, gets cold northerly winds from the Arctic, bringing ice and snow in winter.

Aspect 3: Land and sea - continentality.
The sea heats and cools slowly and stores heat, so coastal areas have mild winters and cool summers. Ireland averages about 6 degrees C in winter and 16 degrees C in summer.
Land heats and cools quickly. Places far from the sea have extreme temperatures. Samara in Russia, at the same latitude as Ireland, averages -14 degrees C in winter and 28 degrees C in summer, a range of 42 degrees C.
Oymyakon in Russia, the coldest inhabited place, has reached -67.8 degrees C.

Aspect 4: Altitude.
Most heat in the atmosphere radiates from the Earth's surface, so the air is warmer near the ground.
Temperature falls about 1 degree C for every 150 m of height (the lapse rate), because air at height is less dense and holds less heat.
So Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, although on the equator, has snow on its 5,895 m summit.

Conclusion: latitude, ocean currents and winds, distance from the sea and altitude together cause the uneven distribution of temperature across the Earth's surface.

prompt:
23. Exchanges of water between oceans and atmosphere, over the earth's surface, impact on precipitation and its distribution patterns.
Discuss.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Water moves between the oceans and the atmosphere. Heat evaporates water from the sea into water vapour, winds carry it over the land, and it cools and condenses to form clouds and precipitation. Where this happens decides where it is wet and where it is dry.

Aspect 1: Convectional rainfall in the tropics.
Near the equator the north-east and south-east trade winds meet and are forced upwards, forming low pressure.
Intense heat evaporates a great deal of moisture. The warm, moist air rises, cools and condenses, giving heavy convectional rain, often in the afternoon.
Tropical areas such as Brazil and Papua New Guinea get about 200 days of rain a year and 2,000 to 10,000 mm annually, with humidity of about 83%.
About half of this rain comes from plants. Trees release water vapour through transpiration (evapotranspiration), which rises, condenses and falls again. Each tree releases about 755 litres of water a year.

Aspect 2: Relief rainfall from moist ocean winds.
Ireland's prevailing south-westerly winds blow over thousands of kilometres of the Atlantic and pick up moisture.
When this moist air meets the mountains of the west coast, it is forced to rise. It cools and condenses, giving relief (orographic) rainfall on the windward side.
On the far side the air descends, warms and becomes drier - the rain shadow.
So the west of Ireland gets about 1,600 mm of rain a year, almost twice the east (about 800 mm). The same pattern explains why the Atacama Desert, on the leeside of the Andes, is the driest desert.

Aspect 3: Cold ocean currents and deserts.
Where cold ocean currents flow, little water evaporates and the air above is cooled.
The Canaries Current off west Africa and the Humboldt (Peru) Current off South America cool winds blowing towards them, so any rain falls at sea and the winds reach land dry.
Together with sinking, dry air in the high-pressure zones between 15 and 30 degrees, this creates hot deserts such as the Sahara and Atacama, which receive 0 to 250 mm of rain a year and have humidity of 10% or less.

Aspect 4: Mid-latitude cyclones and polar regions.
In the mid-latitudes, depressions form over the Atlantic and carry moist ocean air towards land. At the cold front, warm air is forced up quickly, giving intense, short-lived rain; at the warm front there is long-lasting light rain. Ireland gets about five such cyclones a year, bringing heavy rain and strong winds, and rain falls all year with no dry season.
In polar regions, cold air holds very little moisture and evaporation is low, so precipitation is under 250 mm a year and these areas are classed as deserts.

Conclusion: the amount of water exchanged between the ocean and the atmosphere, and how it is lifted and cooled, creates the global pattern of wet tropics and west coasts and dry deserts and poles.

prompt:
24. Describe and account for the characteristics of one global climate type that you have studied.
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Climate type: the cool temperate oceanic climate (Koppen type C), found between about 30 and 60 degrees north and south, e.g. Ireland and parts of New Zealand.

Aspect 1: Mild temperatures with no extremes - and why.
Winters are mild, averaging about 6 degrees C, and summers are cool to warm, averaging about 16 degrees C. There are four distinct seasons but no extremes.
The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry warm tropical water north. They warm the air above, and the prevailing winds carry this warmth onto land, raising winter temperatures and keeping coasts ice-free. Without them, Western Europe would have much colder winters.
The sea heats and cools slowly and stores heat. Sea air masses release this heat in winter, so coastal areas stay mild. By contrast, Samara in Russia, at the same latitude but far from the sea, averages -14 degrees C in winter.

Aspect 2: Seasonal changes caused by latitude.
Being in the mid-latitudes, the angle of the sun changes during the year.
In summer the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the sun, so rays are more direct and concentrated and days are longer, giving warmer weather.
In winter it is tilted away, the rays are spread over a larger area and days are shorter, so it is colder.

Aspect 3: Rain all year round - and why.
Cool temperate areas receive 800 to 2,000 mm of rain a year, with no distinct wet or dry season.
The prevailing south-westerly winds blow from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic, bringing mild, moist ocean air.
About five mid-latitude cyclones a year bring heavy rain and strong winds. Warm and cold fronts force warm, moist air to rise, cool and condense.
Ireland is affected by several air masses, such as Tropical Maritime air, which is warm and moist, bringing cloud and rain, and Polar Maritime air, which is cold and showery.

Aspect 4: Uneven distribution of rainfall - relief and rain shadow.
When moist Atlantic air meets the western mountains, it is forced to rise, cools and condenses, giving relief rainfall on the windward side.
The air descends on the far side and becomes drier, creating a rain shadow.
So the west of Ireland gets about 1,600 mm a year, almost twice the east (about 800 mm). The east also has less cloud, giving a growing season of about 280 days, over a month longer than the western seaboard.

Conclusion: the cool temperate oceanic climate is mild, moist and changeable because of its mid-latitude position, warm ocean currents, the moderating sea and moist south-westerly winds. This climate supports Ireland's green, grassy landscape and deciduous woodland.

prompt:
Question 1
1B. Tectonic Activity - Irish Landscape
Examine how tectonic activity has influenced the development of the Irish landscape.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Tectonic activity has shaped the Irish landscape through folding, volcanic activity and metamorphism.

Influence 1 - Caledonian folding formed fold mountains. About 420 million years ago the North American Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate, closing the Iapetus Ocean. Neither plate was dense enough to be subducted, so horizontal compression buckled and uplifted sea-floor sediments into anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds). This formed the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains. Magma was forced up into the folds and cooled slowly to form the Leinster Batholith, a granite core over 120 km long. Its heat baked the surrounding shale and sandstone into schist, slate and quartzite. Weathering and erosion later stripped away the cover, exposing rounded granite peaks such as Kippure, while resistant schist forms Lugnaquilla (925 m).

Influence 2 - Armorican folding. About 250 million years ago the African and Eurasian plates collided, forming a chain of fold mountains across western Europe. In Ireland this produced the MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry, where Carrauntoohil (1,038 m) is Ireland's highest mountain. At Loughshinny, Co. Dublin, crustal movements about 300 million years ago squeezed flat layers of limestone and shale into V-shaped chevron folds.

Influence 3 - Volcanic activity at a divergent boundary. About 65 million years ago, as the Eurasian and North American plates separated, runny basic lava poured out of long cracks (fissure eruptions). Layer upon layer of basalt built up to 1 km thick, forming the flat Antrim Plateau. As the lava cooled it contracted and cracked into about 40,000 hexagonal columns - the Giant's Causeway.

prompt:
Question 1
1C. Human Interaction with the Rock Cycle
Examine how humans interact with the rock cycle, with reference to one of the following:
- Mining
- Extraction of building materials
- Oil/gas exploitation
- Geothermal energy production.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Geothermal energy production - Iceland.

Humans interact with the rock cycle by tapping the heat of magma and hot rocks below the surface (endogenic processes). Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates pull apart, and also on a hotspot. Magma rises close to the surface through fissures and heats the surrounding rock and groundwater.

Interaction 1 - Producing electricity and heat. Water heated by hot rocks underground is used to generate electricity and heat buildings. Geothermal energy supplies electricity to 90% of Icelandic homes, plus greenhouses, swimming pools and industries. It is clean, renewable and affordable, so Iceland needs fewer imported fossil fuels and has cut its CO2 emissions by up to 37%.

Interaction 2 - Supporting the economy. Cheap geothermal energy gives energy-intensive industries such as aluminium smelting a competitive edge. Greenhouses heated by geothermal energy grow vegetables and flowers all year, cutting expensive food imports. Geothermal pools such as the Blue Lagoon attract tourists.

Interaction 3 - Living with an active rock cycle. Geothermal plants sit on active volcanic ground, so new lava can threaten them. Lava barriers and protective dykes were built around the Svartsengi geothermal plant on the Reykjanes Peninsula, where eruptions in 2023-2024 destroyed houses in Grindavik. Monitoring and emergency planning add ongoing costs.

A second example is the Philippines, on the Pacific Ring of Fire, which uses hot rocks under volcanoes such as Mayon and ranks third in the world for geothermal electricity.

prompt:
Question 2
2B. Surface Processes
Answer (i) or (ii)
(i) Examine the role of the processes of erosion on the formation of one fluvial landform or one coastal landform or one glacial landform that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Landform: sea cliff and wave-cut platform, e.g. the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare.

Hydraulic action: destructive waves (more than ten per minute, with a stronger backwash) crash against the base of the cliff, especially in gales and storms. The force of the water is driven into cracks, joints and bedding planes, widening them until pieces of rock fall away.

Compressed air: as a wave strikes, air is trapped in cracks a fraction of a second before the water. The air is compressed, and when the backwash retreats the pressure is released explosively, shattering the rock.

Abrasion: waves hurl stones and sand at the cliff between the high and low water marks. This exposes weaknesses and cuts a wave-cut notch at the base of the cliff.

Solution: weak carbonic acid in sea water dissolves calcium carbonate where the cliff is made of limestone.

Formation: the notch grows deeper and the rock above is left without support (undercutting). Eventually the overhang collapses under gravity, leaving a steep, vertical cliff face. The fallen rocks are broken down by attrition and become tools for more abrasion. This is repeated again and again, so the cliff retreats inland. The more resistant rock left behind at the base forms a flat wave-cut platform, exposed at low tide and smoothed by attrition. The platform absorbs incoming wave energy and so protects the cliff, which becomes inactive once it has retreated out of reach of the sea. Another example is Sliabh Liag, Co. Donegal - at 601 m, the highest sea cliffs in Europe.

prompt:
Question 2
2C. Metamorphic Rocks
Examine the formation of metamorphic rocks, with reference to examples from Ireland.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Named rocks: marble and quartzite.

Metamorphic rocks form when an existing rock (igneous, sedimentary or older metamorphic) is changed by great heat, pressure or both. The rock does not melt, but its structure, minerals and texture change. This is called metamorphism, an endogenic process.

Heat: high temperatures from nearby magma or deep burial make minerals recrystallise or form new minerals. When hot magma forces its way into cooler rock, this is contact (thermal) metamorphism, and the changed zone around the intrusion is the aureole. Pressure: deep burial or mountain building squeezes and folds rocks, lining minerals up in parallel bands (foliation). Combined heat and pressure over large areas where plates collide is regional metamorphism.

Marble: limestone formed from shells and bones rich in calcium carbonate on the seabed. During the Caledonian orogeny, about 450 million years ago, tectonic activity forced it deep underground. Temperatures of 500-800 degrees C and great pressure over millions of years recrystallised the calcite, removing fossils and forming a hard, dense, non-foliated rock. Impurities give colour: Connemara marble, Co. Galway, is green (serpentine) and Kilkenny marble is black (carbon).

Quartzite: sandstone made of quartz grains. About 400 million years ago, when the Eurasian and North American plates collided, magma squeezed between folded layers and superheated the sandstone (contact metamorphism). The quartz grains recrystallised and cemented together into a very hard rock that resists erosion. Examples: the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow, and Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo.

Similarly, heat from the Leinster Batholith baked shale into slate and schist in the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains.

prompt:
Question 3
3B. Weathering
Explain the role of temperature in the process(es) of physical/mechanical weathering.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals. Temperature change is the key driver of two processes: freeze-thaw action and exfoliation.

Freeze-thaw action (e.g. Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo): this happens in upland areas where temperatures rise above and fall below freezing. By day (e.g. 10 degrees C) rainwater seeps into cracks and joints in the rock. At night the temperature drops below 0 degrees C (e.g. -3 degrees C) and the water freezes. Ice expands by about 9% in volume, putting pressure on the rock and widening the crack. When the temperature rises again the ice thaws and water seeps deeper. This repeated freezing and thawing eventually breaks pieces off. The loose, angular fragments collect on steep slopes as scree. Freeze-thaw also weathers the sides of V-shaped valleys in upland river courses.

Exfoliation (e.g. the Sahara Desert): this happens in hot deserts with a large diurnal temperature range. Because there is little cloud, up to 90% of the sun's rays reach the ground by day, heating the outer layer of rock to about 40 degrees C so it expands. At night the heat escapes quickly and temperatures can drop to about -10 degrees C, so the outer layer cools and contracts. This daily expansion and contraction stresses the outer layer; cracks form, join up, and the outer layer peels away like the skin of an onion. This is why exfoliation is also called 'onion peeling'.

In both processes it is the repeated change in temperature, not one hot or cold day, that causes the rock to break down.

prompt:
Question 3
3C. Human Interaction with Surface Processes
'Human activity impacts on surface processes.'
Examine this statement with reference to one of the following:
- The impact of dams on river processes
- The impact of coastal defence work on coastal processes
- The impact of human activity on mass movement.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Coastal defence work changes the processes of erosion, transportation and deposition. Example: Salthill, Co. Galway (hard engineering) and Enniscrone, Co. Sligo (soft engineering).

Impact 1 - Rock armour reduces erosion. Galway City Council placed large boulders in a gradual slope in front of old, near-vertical sea walls at Salthill. The rocks absorb and reduce the energy of breaking waves, which stops hydraulic action and abrasion attacking the coast.

Impact 2 - Recurved sea walls reflect waves. The curve and lip of a wave-return wall fling the swash back out to sea in storm surges, so the backwash cannot erode the beach in front. Steps on some walls absorb wave energy and make waves break early. Such walls are very effective but expensive - 1 m of sea wall costs more than 1 m of motorway - and they damage habitats and scenery.

Impact 3 - Groynes interrupt longshore drift. Boulder groynes at right angles to the shore at Salthill trap sand moving sideways along the coast, so the beach is kept in place. However, they starve areas further down the coast of sediment, so erosion increases there.

Impact 4 - Soft engineering encourages deposition. At Enniscrone, where the dunes are about 5 km long, porous fencing traps blown sand so dunes build up behind it, and marram grass slows the wind so sand is deposited. Boardwalks and rerouted paths stop trampling, which otherwise creates wind tunnels that blow sand inland. Fencing costs only 5 to 25 euro per metre, and the dunes absorb wave energy as a natural flood defence.

prompt:
Question 4
4C. Concept of a Region
Examine how culture or climate can be used to define regions, with reference to an example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Climate can define regions because places with similar average temperature and precipitation over 30 years or more form distinct climate zones. In 1884 Wladimir Koppen grouped the world into five major zones based on temperature and precipitation: Tropical (A), Arid (B), Temperate (C), Continental (D) and Polar (E), divided into 30 subzones.

Example 1 - Ireland, a cool temperate oceanic region (Type C). Winters average about 6 degrees C and summers about 16 degrees C, with 800 to 2,000 mm of rain spread through the year and no dry season. This is caused by mid-latitude location, warm south-westerly winds and the Gulf Stream/North Atlantic Drift, which keep winters mild. These shared conditions make Ireland one climate region.

Example 2 - the Mediterranean, a warm temperate region, e.g. southern Spain. Summers are hot and dry (about 28 degrees C in July) because of subtropical high pressure, while winters are mild and wet (about 10 degrees C in January) as the polar front shifts south. Rainfall is only 400 to 700 mm. This climate defines the region and also its economy, as the 'sun and sea' attracts mass tourism to the Costa del Sol.

Example 3 - hot desert regions between 15 and 30 degrees north and south, such as the Sahara. They are defined by aridity: 0 to 250 mm of rain a year and a diurnal range from 0 to 45 degrees C, caused by sinking air in high pressure, cold ocean currents and rain shadows.

Limitations: Koppen uses only temperature and precipitation and ignores extreme events, so boundaries between climate regions are not sharp lines but gradual changes.

topic_label: Farming in the West of Ireland
prompt:
Question 6
6B. Agriculture in Ireland
Account for the development of agriculture in an Irish region that you have studied, with reference to any two of the following factors:
- Relief
- Climate
- Markets.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Region: the West of Ireland (Western Region).

Factor 1 - Relief. The West has rugged Caledonian fold mountains such as the Ox Mountains (Sligo), the Nephin Beg Range (Mayo) and the Twelve Pins (Galway). Steep slopes make it hard to use machinery and to build transport networks, for example around Croagh Patrick. Severe glacial erosion during the last Ice Age stripped away soil, leaving rocky, infertile uplands, and poor drainage causes waterlogging. As a result, farms are small, averaging 25.5 hectares compared with a national average of 32.5 hectares. Farmers keep less profitable sheep and dry stock cattle (fattened for beef) on rough grazing, and less than 2% of Irish cereal was grown in the West in 2023. Over half of western farmers work part-time and almost two-thirds of western farms are not economically viable.

Factor 2 - Climate. The West has a cool temperate oceanic climate, with mild winters (5-6 degrees C) and summers of 15-16 degrees C. Moist south-westerly winds from the Atlantic rise over the western mountains, causing relief rainfall of about 1,600 mm a year - almost twice the 800 mm of the East. This high rainfall suits grass growth, so pastoral farming dominates. However, it causes leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease, which limit cereal growing, and very high rainfall has formed infertile blanket bogs on the mountains. More cloud also means a shorter growing season - the East has about 280 days, over a month longer than the western seaboard. Climate change brings longer grass-growing seasons but also more storms and flooding that damage farms.

Economic activities: agriculture and fishing in Ireland.

Agriculture: intensive dairy and beef farming increase greenhouse gases - methane from livestock and nitrous oxide from nitrogen fertilisers - and nutrient runoff of nitrates and phosphates from slurry pollutes rivers and lakes. To control this, Food Vision 2030 aims to make Ireland a leader in sustainable food systems. Farmers are encouraged to rewet land to trap carbon, reduce herd sizes, plant legumes such as peas and beans that need no fertiliser, and grow cover crops that trap nutrients. Organic farming has tripled in area since 2020, using crop rotation and integrated pest management (e.g. ladybirds) instead of chemicals. Precision agriculture uses sensors and GPS to apply exactly the right amount of fertiliser and water, reducing waste. EU schemes such as ACRES pay farmers to improve biodiversity, climate, air and water quality.

Fishing: in the late 1970s foreign trawlers overfished Irish waters and herring and cod were almost wiped out. The EU Common Fisheries Policy now controls this. Total Allowable Catch quotas limit how much each state can catch, and Maximum Sustainable Yield is set by marine biologists so that future stocks are not reduced. The minimum mesh size was increased to 100 mm so young fish escape, and the Irish Conservation Box protects spawning grounds of cod, herring and whiting. Since 2019 the landing obligation bans wasteful discarding. These measures have prevented the collapse of many species while keeping the industry viable.

Question 8
8B. Globalisation
Explain the impact of globalisation on one developing economy that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Developing economy: China.

Impact 1 - Rapid economic growth through trade and investment. Once a closed economy, China became business-friendly as the WTO and IMF encouraged countries to reduce trade barriers. The free flow of capital led to a surge in foreign direct investment, and container shipping made exporting cheap. China grew into a global superpower in trade and is now the world's second-largest economy (about 18.5 trillion US dollars in 2024). Hundreds of millions of people have been lifted out of poverty, and China invests abroad through its Belt and Road Initiative, e.g. a loan of 200 million US dollars to Cote d'Ivoire for cocoa factories.

Impact 2 - Urbanisation and rural-to-urban migration. Factory jobs drew millions from the countryside to cities. Shenzhen grew rapidly between 1982 and today, and Chongqing is now an ultramodern city of over 32 million people. Beijing had 77,000 cars and 5.6 million bikes in 1978, but by 2018 cars had largely replaced bikes, showing rising incomes.

Impact 3 - Inequality and environmental pressure. Wealth is unevenly shared between richer cities and poorer rural areas. Overcrowding and rapid city growth create environmental pressures.

Impact 4 - Vulnerability to global events. Because China depends on world trade, it is exposed to decisions elsewhere: in April 2025 the US placed its highest tariffs on Chinese goods, sparking threats of a trade war.

Developed economy: Spain - mass tourism.

The south and east coasts (Costa Brava, Costa del Sol) have a Mediterranean climate: long, hot, dry summers of about 28 degrees C in July and mild winters of about 10 degrees C. Political factors - government planning and investment. After World War II the Spanish government used tourism to rebuild the economy. The Ministry of Tourism's 'Spain is Different' campaign promoted the climate, beaches and culture, and Spain was marketed as a low-risk package-holiday destination. The state invested in airports such as Malaga, motorways, coastal roads, the high-speed LAV rail network and water, electricity and sewerage in resorts. Fewer than 1 million tourists came in 1950; by the 1970s there were over 30 million a year, and a record 94 million in 2024. Tourism now provides nearly 3 million jobs and 15% of GDP. 9C. European Union Policy
Examine how different European Union policies impact on the Irish economy.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Policies: the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP).

CAP: introduced in 1962 and applied in Ireland from 1973. Guaranteed minimum prices for milk, beef and cereals and headage payments (1975) caused a big rise in output and farm incomes. Irish farming changed from small subsistence farms to specialised, export-focused dairy and beef farms. Agriculture is now worth a record 17 billion euro (8% of GDP), employs almost 10% of the workforce, and 90% of Irish beef is exported. The abolition of milk quotas in 2015 made Irish dairying the fastest-growing dairy market in the EU. Negative impact: EU sugar reforms in 2006 cut the sugar price by 36%, cheap imports flooded in, over 3,700 sugar beet farmers were affected and the Carlow and Mallow plants closed, destroying the Irish sugar industry. Today schemes such as ACRES and TAMS pay farmers for environmental work.

CFP: introduced in 1983. Ireland had to share its waters, and foreign trawlers almost wiped out herring and cod in the late 1970s. Ireland has about 12% of EU waters but as little as 15% of the catch value from them; 36% of fish landed in Ireland in 2024 were landed by foreign trawlers. Decommissioning caused job losses on the western seaboard. Positive impacts: access to a single market of 450 million consumers (55.9% of Irish seafood went to the EU in 2024, worth 385 million euro); EMFAF funding modernised harbours and processing plants at Killybegs and Baltimore; and quotas protect stocks so the industry, now worth 1.24 billion euro, can survive.

Examine how the functions of urban centres can change over time, with reference to Irish example(s).

model_answer:
Urban centre: Galway City. Functions: defence and trade (commercial).

Defence: in 1232 the Anglo-Normans under Richard Mor de Burgo built a castle at today's Druid Lane, and Galway became a walled town. The wall had five gates with tolls, paid for by taxes on traded goods. By 1750 the walls were in disrepair and by 1800 they were gone, so the defence function was lost.

Trade/commerce: from about 1400 fourteen merchant families, the 'Tribes of Galway', grew wealthy through trade, and commerce became the main function, with a market around Mainguard Street. Under English rule from 1652 trade declined, but the Eyre family built a quay and dock at the Long Walk around 1750, adding a port function.

Industry and education: in the 19th century grain mills, warehouses, breweries and distilleries were built along the Corrib. Queen's College opened in 1845 (now the University of Galway), giving an educational function. In 1967 the first industrial estate opened at Mervue, and Digital employed 1,200 people directly before closing in 1993. Today Boston Scientific and Medtronic make Galway a MedTech hub, using its educated workforce.

Tourism: the railway from Dublin arrived in 1851 with the Railway Hotel, and Salthill grew as a seaside resort. Tourism grew further after Shannon Airport and the M6, and Galway is now a festival city (Galway Races, Arts Festival). Galway has changed from a defended trading town into a modern multifunctional city.

Question 11
11C. Population Characteristics - Ireland
Describe and explain how the characteristics of Ireland's population have changed since the 1950's.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Change 1 - Population size has grown. Ireland had about 2.9 million people in 1950 and about 5.4 million in 2025. In the 1960s the population began to grow for the first time in over 120 years, as government policies attracted multinationals and reduced emigration. Joining the EEC in 1973 brought more trade and jobs. Growth slowed in the 1980s recession, when over 200,000 young adults emigrated, but rose quickly in the Celtic Tiger years (1995-2008).

Change 2 - Birth rates and family size have fallen. In 1961 the fertility rate was 3.78 and the Catholic Church encouraged large families. The marriage bar forced women in some jobs to resign on marriage until 1973. Since then equal pay laws, more women in third-level education and work, and the availability of contraception have led to smaller families. The fertility rate is now about 1.5, below the replacement level of 2.1, and first-time mothers are over 31 on average, compared with 26 in the 1980s.

Change 3 - The population is ageing. Life expectancy is now about 83 because of better healthcare and living standards. About 15.7% were aged 65 or over in 2022, and this could reach 30% by 2050. This raises pension and healthcare costs.

Change 4 - Migration and diversity. Ireland changed from a donor to a receiver country. Migration was the main cause of population change from 2016 to 2024, with migrants from Poland, India and Ukraine, mostly aged 25-44. Ireland is now multicultural, and growth is concentrated in urban areas in the east, while the remote west still loses people.

Global Interdependence
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
14. Examine how social and/or political decisions can impact on each of the following:
- Economic and political refugees
- Human rights issues.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Social and political decisions made by governments and international bodies have a huge impact on refugees and on human rights.

Aspect 1 - Political decisions that create refugees: the war in Ukraine. Russia's decision to launch a large-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 caused one of the largest refugee crises in recent history. Over 6.8 million refugees fled, about 92% of them to other European countries, and about 8 million people became internally displaced within Ukraine. About 90% of those who left were women and children, because the Ukrainian government decided that most men aged 18-60 must stay for military service. This split families apart. The EU then made the political decision to open its borders through the Temporary Protection scheme, giving Ukrainians housing, education and the right to work. Almost 120,000 Ukrainians have moved to Ireland. However, uneven burden sharing means Germany, Poland and Czechia host about half of Ukrainians in the EU and complain of strained capacity.

Aspect 2 - Decisions about who counts as a refugee: climate and economic migrants. Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a 'climate refugee' is not recognised, so countries have no legal duty to accept people displaced by climate disaster. In the Sahel, drought, failed rains and desertification force people to leave their land; UNHCR says displaced people there are rising to 5 million. Because they are treated as economic migrants, they have no legal protection. Political decisions in host countries also matter: Italy and Hungary elected anti-migrant parties, and far-right parties such as the AfD in Germany blame immigrants for social problems. Ireland's government chose a different path, setting up a Department of Home Affairs and passing the International Protection Bill (2025) to make the asylum system faster and fairer, while the EU Migration and Asylum Pact requires refugees to apply in the first EU country they enter.

Aspect 3 - Political decisions and human rights: Afghanistan under the Taliban. The Taliban government rules by a strict interpretation of sharia law that limits freedoms, especially for women and minorities. It closed girls' secondary schools and restricted women's university education and work. In 2023 about 3.7 million children were not in school. These decisions keep Afghanistan's HDI among the lowest in the world (0.462, rank 182). Decades of conflict and unstable government have also forced over 3 million Afghans to flee since 2001, living as refugees in neighbouring countries where girls often cannot attend school. Human rights can also be improved by decisions: Irish Aid supports an initiative in the Afar region of Ethiopia to tackle female genital mutilation and child marriage, and the UN's SDG 5 aims to end discrimination and violence against women and girls.

Conclusion: whether people are forced to flee, whether they are protected when they arrive, and whether their basic rights are respected all depend on social and political decisions.

15. Examine sustainable development as a model for future development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Sustainable development aims to improve quality of life by solving problems like hunger, poverty and pollution without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

Aspect 1 - The three pillars and the SDGs. Sustainable development rests on three interconnected pillars: environmental (protecting clean air, water and forests), economic (building a stable economy with jobs and businesses) and social (fairness and equity, reducing poverty). Good solutions should help all three. The UN Sustainable Development Goals set worldwide targets, such as ending poverty, fighting climate change and ensuring clean water and good health for everyone. Unlike modernisation, which tells poorer countries to copy richer ones and can damage the environment, or protectionism, which can raise prices and cause trade wars, sustainable development balances nature, people and money. Its weakness is that it takes time and is harder to put into practice.

Aspect 2 - A model country: Finland. Finland ranked first on the 2025 SDG Index. It balances economic growth with environmental protection and social equity, prioritising waste recycling, clean transport, health and education. It aims to be carbon neutral by 2035 by cutting emissions and strengthening carbon sinks. This shows that a wealthy, developed country can grow while protecting its environment, offering a model for others.

Aspect 3 - Sustainable development in Ireland. The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040) is built on National Strategic Outcomes based on the SDGs. It promotes compact growth, with 50% of new city homes on brownfield, derelict and vacant sites, to stop urban sprawl destroying farmland. All new developments must be Transport Orientated Developments, such as Clonburris in South Dublin, 12 minutes from the city by rail. In farming, Food Vision 2030 aims to make Ireland a world leader in sustainable food, with reduced herd sizes, legumes that need no fertiliser and the rewetting of land to trap carbon. Organic farming tripled in area between 2020 and 2026.

Aspect 4 - Global cooperation on climate. Sustainable development needs countries to work together. Under the Paris Agreement (2015), 196 countries agreed to keep warming well below 2 degrees C and aim for 1.5 degrees C, with the overall aim of net zero. Every country must report its emissions and set more ambitious targets every five years. Actions include switching from fossil fuels to wind, solar and geothermal power, district heating as in Sweden (where only 2% of emissions come from heating buildings), and planting forests as carbon sinks. However, the model is fragile: the US withdrew from the Paris Agreement in January 2025, showing that sustainable development depends on political will.

Conclusion: by balancing the economy, society and the environment, sustainable development is the best model for a fairer, safer future.

prompt:
Geoecology
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
16. Explain how soil characteristics impact on soil development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Soil characteristics such as organic matter, texture and structure, water and air content, and pH strongly affect how a soil develops. Ireland's four main soils - brown earths, gleys, podzols and peat - show this clearly.

Aspect 1 - Organic matter (humus). Humus is a dark, jelly-like substance formed from decayed organic matter. In brown earth soils, e.g. in Co. Wexford, mild temperatures let earthworms, insects, fungi and bacteria recycle leaf litter for most of the year. Rapid decomposition gives a high humus content and a dark colour. Worms mix organic and mineral matter, so there are no sharp layers. High humus means brown earths do not waterlog in heavy rain and never fully dry out, making them fertile and ideal for arable farming. In contrast, in peat soils the lack of oxygen stops microbes decomposing plant litter, so sphagnum moss builds up faster than it decays, forming deep, infertile, acidic bogs.

Aspect 2 - Texture and structure. Brown earths developed on glacial deposits about 10,000 years old, giving a loamy texture (a balance of sand, silt and clay) and a granular structure of rounded, grain-like particles. This makes them well-drained and well-aerated with good percolation, so roots grow deeply and the soil develops into a mature, fertile profile. Gley soils, e.g. in Cavan, Monaghan, Leitrim and Clare, form over impermeable bedrock with a high clay content. They have a blocky structure of cube-shaped particles because of constant waterlogging. This restricts roots and limits oxygen, so gleys are only moderately fertile.

Aspect 3 - Water and air (drainage and aeration). Waterlogged gley soils undergo anaerobic reduction: micro-organisms use up the oxygen, and chemical reactions turn iron a bluish-grey colour, which is leached down the profile. In podzols, e.g. in Counties Cork and Cavan, heavy rainfall causes severe leaching that washes nutrients out of the topsoil, leaving an ash-grey layer. Iron and organic matter build up lower down to form a hardpan (iron pan), which makes the soil poorly drained and easily waterlogged. Because brown earths are in areas of lower rainfall (about 800 mm in Dublin), there is little leaching and they stay well-drained.

Aspect 4 - pH (acidity). Brown earths range from slightly alkaline to slightly acidic, which is ideal for microbes, so decomposition and nutrient recycling are rapid. Podzols are acidic, partly because coniferous needles provide poor litter, forming raw acid humus (mor) with little microbial action. Peat is also acidic, which further limits microbes and helps preserve dead matter. Acidic soils therefore develop slowly and stay infertile.

Conclusion: soil characteristics interact with each other - good structure, high humus and a balanced pH produce fertile, mature soils, while poor drainage, leaching and acidity produce infertile ones.

prompt:
Geoecology
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
17. With reference to one biome that you have studied, account for the type of climate experienced in this biome and explain how this climate impacts on soils and vegetation within the biome.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Biome: Ireland's temperate deciduous rainforest biome.

Aspect 1 - The climate and its causes. Ireland has a cool temperate oceanic climate. Average temperatures are about 6 degrees C in winter and 16 degrees C in summer, with no extremes. Precipitation of 800 to 1,600 mm is spread evenly through the year, so there is no dry season. This is caused by warm south-westerly prevailing winds, the warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift, and the moderating effect of the Atlantic Ocean, which stores heat and releases it slowly in winter. Moist air masses such as Tropical Maritime and Polar Maritime converge over Ireland. When moist Atlantic air rises over the western mountains it cools and condenses, giving relief rainfall, so the west gets about 1,600 mm and the east, in the rain shadow, about 800 mm.

Aspect 2 - Impact of climate on soils. In the drier, warmer, brighter south and east, brown earth soils formed under deciduous forest. Mild temperatures mean the ground rarely freezes, so earthworms, fungi and bacteria recycle leaf litter for most of the year, giving a high humus content and a dark colour. Low rainfall means little leaching, so they are fertile and well-drained - ideal for arable farming. In the wetter west, heavy rainfall causes leaching and waterlogging. Podzols form under conifers, with an ash-grey leached layer and an iron pan. Gley soils form where drainage is poor, turning bluish-grey through anaerobic reduction. Where rain is heaviest and the ground is waterlogged, lack of oxygen stops decomposition and peat soils form. Ireland has 8% of the world's blanket bogs.

Aspect 3 - Impact of climate on vegetation. The mild, damp climate gives a long growing season and year-round greenness. The biome is dominated by broadleaf deciduous trees such as oak, ash, alder, birch and hazel. Sessile oaks, as in Killarney National Park, have wide, flat leaves to capture sunlight in cloudy conditions and shed them in autumn to reduce water loss and avoid storm damage; the fallen leaves form humus. The woodland is layered: emergents up to 40 m, a canopy of about 20 m, an understorey of hazel, holly and hawthorn, a field layer of bluebells, wild garlic and ferns, and a ground layer of mosses and liverworts. Bluebells and wild garlic flower in spring before the canopy closes. Constant moisture and high humidity let mosses, lichens and epiphytes cling to trees - 51% of European liverworts occur in Ireland. Ivy has waxy leaves and stays green all year. Because winters are not harsh and summers are not hot enough for drought stress, moisture-loving species thrive.

Conclusion: Ireland's mild, wet oceanic climate explains its fertile brown earths in the east, its leached and waterlogged soils in the west, and its lush, layered deciduous woodland.

prompt:
Culture and Identity
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
20. Examine the effects of political and/or physical boundaries on cultural groups.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Political boundaries, drawn by governments, can divide, displace or protect cultural groups.

Aspect 1 - The Partition of India, 1947. When Britain granted independence to British India, it divided the land along religious and cultural lines into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan (West and East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh in 1971). Local leaders decided which country their province joined. The new boundary left Muslim minorities in India and Hindu minorities in Pakistan, which led to riots. About 12 million people fled Pakistan for India and over 10 million went the other way, and about 1 million died in violent clashes. The boundary split communities, created huge refugee flows and left lasting bitterness between the two religious groups.

Aspect 2 - Kashmir and the Line of Control. Kashmir's leader, Maharaja Hari Singh, chose to join India in 1947, even though 80% of the people were Muslims who wanted to join Pakistan. War broke out, and the UN brought an uneasy peace: western Kashmir went to Pakistan and the east stayed with India. The ceasefire line, the Line of Control, was agreed in 1949. This boundary divides the Kashmiri people. Wars followed in 1965 and 1999, and attacks continue, such as the 2025 attack on tourists at Pahalgam and India's Operation Sindoor in response. In 2019 the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act redrew internal boundaries into Jammu and Kashmir and Buddhist-majority Ladakh, aiming to increase Hindu control and reduce Muslim influence, which caused outrage. Kashmiris suffer persecution from both sides, tourism collapses after violence, and in the 1990s hundreds of thousands fled the Kashmir Valley to Delhi and Jammu.

Aspect 3 - The Gaeltacht: a boundary that protects a cultural group. After the 1950s Irish was mainly spoken in Gaeltacht areas of Galway, Kerry and Donegal. Lack of jobs led young people to leave, so Irish-speaking communities such as Connemara declined. Today the Gaeltacht boundary is used to protect the language. Under the Galway County Development Plan 2022-2028, planning permission in An Ghaeltacht is given to people who can prove they speak Irish. Udaras na Gaeltachta supports jobs inside the boundary, for example helping business parks switch to renewable energy, and community hubs such as GTEIC in An Tearmann, Co. Donegal, let remote workers stay in Gaeltacht villages. Here a boundary helps a cultural group survive rather than dividing it.

Conclusion: political boundaries drawn without respect for cultural groups, as in India and Kashmir, cause conflict and displacement, while boundaries designed around a culture, like the Gaeltacht, can help preserve it.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
22. 'Climate characteristics have an influence on economic development.'
Discuss this statement with reference to each of the following:
- Agriculture
- Drought and desertification
- Tourism.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1 - Agriculture in Ireland. Ireland's cool temperate oceanic climate has mild winters (5-6 degrees C), mild summers (15-16 degrees C) and rain all year. Rain is not evenly spread: moist south-westerly winds rise over western mountains, giving the west about 1,600 mm a year, almost twice the 800 mm of the east and south-east, which lie in the rain shadow. In the west, high rainfall suits grass, so pastoral farming of sheep and dry stock cattle dominates, but leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease limit cereals. Farms are small and almost two-thirds are not economically viable. The drier, sunnier east has a growing season of about 280 days - over a month longer than the west - so it supports large, commercial cereal and vegetable farms that supply firms such as Guinness and Tayto. Overall, the mild climate helps make agriculture worth a record 17 billion euro, with 90% of Irish beef exported. Climate change brings a longer grass-growing season but also new diseases like bluetongue and storm damage.

Aspect 2 - Drought and desertification in the Sahel and Malawi. The Sahel, a semi-arid zone across parts of Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso, Chad and Sudan, is becoming hotter and drier. Failed rains and desertification - fertile land drying out and turning to dust - mean people can no longer depend on farming. Crop failure and livestock deaths increase poverty and food insecurity, and competition for water causes conflict between herders and farmers. Displaced people in the Sahel are rising to 5 million. In Malawi, where most people are subsistence farmers, unpredictable rainfall and a delayed rainy season cause crop failure; maize production fell by 11.4% between 2023 and 2024. Drought followed by heavy rain causes mudslides and soil erosion. The results are higher food prices, malnutrition, unemployment and lost export earnings, which hold back economic development.

Aspect 3 - Tourism in Spain. Spain's Mediterranean coasts have long, hot, dry summers of about 28 degrees C in July, mild winters of about 10 degrees C and over 300 days of sunshine. This dependable 'sun and sea' attracts northern Europeans. Tourists rose from under 1 million in 1950 to a record 94 million in 2024. Tourism provides nearly 3 million jobs and 15% of GDP, and mild winters of 15-18 degrees C make it a year-round industry. However, climate can also damage the industry: heatwaves of 35-40 degrees C reduce demand in July and August, and droughts and wildfires put pressure on water supplies and infrastructure.

Conclusion: climate shapes what can be farmed, where people can earn a living and where tourists go, so it has a major influence on economic development.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
23. Describe the formation of each of the following and discuss its impact on weather patterns:
- Mid-latitude depressions
- Anticyclones
- Land and sea breezes.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1 - Mid-latitude depressions. Formation: these lows form between about 30 and 60 degrees latitude along the polar front, where cold, dense polar air from the north meets warm, less dense tropical air from the south. A disturbance, often from the jet stream, makes a wave or kink in the front, and a low-pressure centre forms at its apex. The low deepens and the Coriolis Effect makes the air circulate anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere. Warm air rises slowly over cold air at the warm front; behind it, cold air advances faster and undercuts the warm air at the cold front. Finally the cold front catches the warm front (occlusion), the supply of warm, moist air is cut off and the low dies away. Impact: they bring unsettled, wet and windy weather. Ahead of the warm front, cirrus, altostratus and nimbostratus clouds give steady, persistent rain. The cold front forms towering cumulonimbus clouds with heavy showers, sometimes thunder, and a sharp drop in temperature. About five a year hit Ireland, moving west to east. Storm Eowyn (January 2025) brought a gust of 184 km/h at Mace Head, Co. Galway, causing widespread power outages.

Aspect 2 - Anticyclones. Formation: colder, heavier air descends from high altitude and spreads outwards from the centre. The Coriolis Effect deflects it so the system circulates slowly clockwise in the northern hemisphere. Sinking air is compressed and warms, which prevents cloud forming. Impact: isobars are far apart, so there is little wind, and the weather is calm, dry and settled. In summer, hot, dry continental air brings heatwaves and drought - Phoenix Park, Dublin, reached 33 degrees C on 18 July 2022. In winter, clear skies let heat escape, giving frost; a high to the north of Ireland can bring polar continental air from Siberia, as in 'The Beast from the East' (2018), when temperatures fell as low as -18 degrees C. Anticyclones can also act as 'blocking highs', forcing rain-bearing depressions to track around them.

Aspect 3 - Land and sea breezes. Formation: land heats up and cools down quickly, while the sea heats and cools slowly and keeps its heat longer. On a sunny day the land becomes warmer than the sea, so air over the land warms and rises, forming lower pressure. Cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it - a sea breeze. At night the land loses heat quickly and becomes cooler than the sea. Air over the warmer sea rises, and cool air flows from the land out to sea - a land breeze. Impact: sea breezes cool coastal areas on hot days, and the sea acts as a heat store that moderates coastal temperatures, so coasts have smaller temperature ranges than inland areas. This is why Ireland's coastal climate lacks the extremes of continental places like Samara, Russia, which ranges from -14 to 28 degrees C.

Conclusion: depressions, anticyclones and local breezes all form through differences in air pressure and temperature, and together they explain much of Ireland's changeable weather.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
24. Climate characteristics change over space and time.
Discuss.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1 - Change over space: latitude. The sun heats the Earth unequally. At the equator the sun's rays are concentrated on a small area and pass through little atmosphere, so tropical climates average about 27 degrees C all year. Towards the poles the rays arrive at a low angle, spread over a larger area and pass through more atmosphere, so polar winters fall below -50 degrees C. Snow and ice reflect up to 90% of the sun's radiation (high albedo), keeping polar regions cold. Rainfall also changes with latitude: at the equator rising air gives heavy convectional rain of 2,000 to 10,000 mm, while between 15 and 30 degrees sinking air in high pressure creates hot deserts such as the Sahara with 0 to 250 mm.

Aspect 2 - Change over space: oceans, distance from the sea and altitude. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry warm water north, so Ireland has mild winters of about 6 degrees C, while Newfoundland, at a similar latitude, has ice and snow from cold northerly winds. Cold currents such as the Canaries Current dry out winds, helping to form deserts. Inland, continentality gives extremes: Samara, Russia, at the same latitude as Ireland, averages -14 degrees C in winter and 28 degrees C in summer. Climate also changes with height: temperature falls about 1 degree C for every 150 m, so Kilimanjaro has snow although it is on the equator. Mountains also cause rain shadows, as in the Atacama Desert.

Aspect 3 - Change over time: natural climate change. Ice cores show Earth's climate has changed naturally many times, including Ice Ages. Causes include Milankovitch cycles (changes in Earth's orbit on a 100,000-year cycle), continental shifts that place land near the poles, and volcanic eruptions. The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in 1991 released sulphur dioxide that reflected sunlight and cut global temperatures by 0.5 degrees C for almost two years. El Nino and La Nina warm and cool the Pacific Ocean over shorter periods.

Aspect 4 - Change over time: human-induced climate change. Since 1850 burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised greenhouse gas levels. Global temperatures were 1.1 degrees C above pre-industrial levels in 2011-2020 and passed 1.5 degrees C for the first time in 2024. Greenland is losing 200 to 270 gigatons of ice a year, raising sea levels. Fresh meltwater is weakening the AMOC, now at its weakest in about 1,600 years; if it stopped, Ireland and Europe could face more powerful storms, seasonal temperature extremes and severe cold snaps. Extreme events are becoming more common, such as Cyclone Freddy (2023), the longest tropical cyclone ever recorded.

Conclusion: climate varies across the globe because of latitude, oceans, land and altitude, and it changes through time because of both natural factors and, increasingly, human activity.
