prompt:
Igneous Rocks
Explain the formation of two igneous rocks, with reference to Irish examples.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Igneous rocks form when molten rock from deep in the Earth cools and solidifies. Two Irish examples are granite and basalt.

Rock 1: Granite (intrusive), e.g. the Leinster Batholith in the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains.
About 400 million years ago the Eurasian and North American plates collided during the Caledonian Orogeny. Magma formed deep underground at the convergent boundary. It rose into the crust but did not reach the surface, so it formed a huge mass called a batholith. Trapped deep down, the magma cooled very slowly. This allowed large crystals of quartz, feldspar and mica to grow, so granite is coarse-grained and light grey or pink. Heat from the magma baked the shale and sandstone around it into schist and quartzite. Over millions of years weathering and erosion stripped away the rock above, exposing the granite, e.g. Kippure. The Leinster Batholith covers about 1,500 square km.

Rock 2: Basalt (extrusive), e.g. the Giant's Causeway and the Antrim Plateau.
About 60-65 million years ago the Eurasian and North American plates began to separate at a divergent boundary. Runny basic lava, low in silica and gas, flowed quietly out of long cracks called fissures. It spread over large areas in thin layers, building a plateau up to 1 km thick. Contact with air or water cooled the lava quickly, so large crystals could not form, giving fine-grained, dark basalt. As it cooled it contracted and cracked into about 40,000 hexagonal columns at the Giant's Causeway.

Diagram: a labelled cross-section showing a batholith cooling deep underground with a metamorphic aureole around it, and lava flowing from a fissure on the surface.

prompt:
Isostasy
Examine how isostasy has impacted on the Irish landscape, with reference to the fluvial landscape and/or the coastal landscape.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Impact: isostatic change has caused parts of Ireland's coast to sink, drowning river and glacial valleys and speeding up coastal erosion.

Isostasy is the rising or sinking of land as weight is added to or removed from it. During the last Ice Age, thick ice sheets lay on Ireland. Their weight pushed the lithosphere down (loading and subsidence), and the soft mantle beneath flowed away. When the ice melted about 11,000 years ago, the weight was removed. The mantle slowly flowed back and the land began to rise (isostatic rebound). This is still happening today.

Ireland is not rebounding evenly. It is tilting like a capsizing boat: the north is rising and the south is sinking. In the south and southwest, sea level is rising relative to the land. The EPA predicts the southwest coast, from the Dingle Peninsula to Cape Clear, will see sea level rise fastest, at 3.3-4.8 mm a year, compared with 2.2-3.7 mm a year on the northeast coast.

As the south sinks, the sea floods inland up river valleys. Drowned V-shaped river valleys form rias, e.g. Kenmare Bay, Co. Kerry. This links the coastal and fluvial landscapes. Drowned U-shaped glacial valleys form fjords, e.g. Killary Harbour, Co. Galway. Estuaries become wider and longer, and more tidal water reaches deltas, making them less fertile.

Tilting areas also face faster coastal erosion. Waves reach further inland, undermining cliffs and headlands so the coastline retreats. Beaches, sand dunes, spits, bars and lagoons may shrink or disappear. Low-lying areas such as the Shannon Estuary and Cork City face more flooding.

prompt:
Surface Processes
Answer (i) or (ii)
(i) Examine the role of the process of deposition on the formation of one fluvial landform or one coastal landform or one glacial landform that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Landform: a river delta (fluvial). Examples: the Nile Delta, Egypt (arcuate) and the Shannon Estuary, Co. Limerick.

A delta is a deposit of sediment at a river mouth. It is formed by deposition. A river deposits its load when it no longer has the energy to carry it.

In the old-age stage the river flows over a gentle gradient. It is slow and carries a large load of fine sand and silt in suspension. When it enters the sea, friction with the sea water slows it down sharply. It loses energy and must drop its load.

Flocculation helps deposition. When fresh water mixes with salt water, a chemical reaction makes tiny charged clay particles stick together. They become heavier and sink to the sea bed.

A delta only forms where tides and currents are weak, so they cannot carry the sediment away. The sediment builds up in layers (beds). The heaviest sediment is dropped first and travels the shortest distance, forming the topset beds. Medium sediment goes further, forming the foreset beds. The finest clay is carried furthest, forming the bottomset beds.

As the deposits build up above sea level, they block the channel. The river splits into smaller channels called distributaries, which spread the sediment over a wider area. New flat, fertile land is formed.

The shape depends on deposition and wave strength. The Nile Delta is arcuate (fan-shaped), with distributaries in a leaf-vein pattern. The Mississippi is a bird's foot delta, where weak waves let sediment build along a few distributaries.

Diagram: cross-section of a delta showing topset, foreset and bottomset beds, with distributaries on the plan view.

prompt:
Chemical Weathering
Explain, with the aid of a labelled diagram(s), how chemical weathering has shaped one of the following:
- The surface karst landscape
- The underground karst landscape.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Surface karst landscape - example: the Burren, Co. Clare.

Process: carbonation, a type of chemical weathering. Chemical weathering changes the mineral make-up of rock.

The Burren is made of limestone. It formed about 350 million years ago when Ireland lay under a warm, shallow tropical sea. Shells and bones rich in calcium carbonate settled on the sea floor and were compacted and cemented into rock. Limestone has horizontal bedding planes and vertical joints, giving it a blocky structure.

As rain falls, it absorbs carbon dioxide from the air. This forms a weak carbonic acid. When the acid lands on limestone, it reacts with the calcium carbonate. This forms calcium bicarbonate, which is soluble and is carried away in solution.

Limestone is permeable. Rainwater flows down through the joints and along the bedding planes instead of running off the surface. So the acid attacks the joints most. Over thousands of years carbonation widens and deepens the joints and weakens the rock.

This shapes the main surface landform, the limestone pavement. The widened joints become deep, narrow grooves called grikes. The flat blocks of limestone left between them are called clints. Together the clints and grikes form the bare, rocky limestone pavement of the Burren.

Fossils of sea creatures are common in the rock, showing its marine origin.

Diagram: a block of limestone showing bedding planes and vertical joints, rain with CO2 forming carbonic acid, widened joints labelled grikes and blocks labelled clints.

prompt:
The Tectonic Cycle
Explain how the study of plate tectonics has helped us to understand the global distribution of any one of the following:
- Earthquakes
- Volcanoes
- Fold mountains
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Chosen: volcanoes. Examples of distribution: the Pacific Ring of Fire and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

Plate tectonics shows that the Earth's lithosphere is broken into large plates, e.g. the Pacific, Nazca and Eurasian plates. Convection currents in the mantle move the plates. They move apart, collide or slide past each other. Most volcanoes lie along these plate boundaries, not at random.

Divergent boundaries: where plates move apart, the crust stretches and thins and fissures open. Magma rises to fill the gap. This explains the line of volcanoes along mid-ocean ridges, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American plates separate. Iceland is a volcanic island on this ridge. Mid-ocean ridges account for over 70% of global volcanic activity. On land, rift valleys form, e.g. the East African Rift, with volcanoes such as Mt Kilimanjaro.

Convergent boundaries: where a dense oceanic plate meets another plate, it is subducted into the mantle. Water released from the sinking plate lowers the melting point of the mantle, forming magma that rises to the surface. This explains chains of volcanoes parallel to subduction zones. The Nazca Plate sinks under the South American Plate, forming the Andes volcanic arc. Two oceanic plates collide near Japan, forming an island arc. This explains the Pacific Ring of Fire, a horseshoe of volcanoes around the Pacific that holds about 75% of the world's active volcanoes.

Transform boundaries: at the San Andreas Fault plates slide past each other. No magma is produced, so there are no volcanoes.

Hotspots explain volcanoes in the middle of plates, e.g. Hawaii, where a plate moves over a fixed mantle plume.

Diagram: subduction zone with trench, sinking plate, rising magma and volcano.

prompt:
Human Interaction with the Rock Cycle
Examine how humans interact with the rock cycle, with reference to one of the following:
- Mining
- Extraction of building materials
- Oil/gas exploitation
- Geothermal energy production.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Chosen: geothermal energy production. Example: Iceland.

In the rock cycle, endogenic processes create heat deep in the Earth. Magma rises towards the surface and heats the rocks around it. Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American plates move apart, and also on a hotspot. So magma lies close to the surface and the rocks are very hot.

Interaction 1 - using the heat: water seeps underground into hot rock and is heated. Humans drill down and use this hot water and steam to drive turbines and heat buildings. Geothermal energy supplies electricity to 90% of Icelandic homes, as well as greenhouses, swimming pools and industries.

This brings economic benefits. Iceland needs fewer imported fossil fuels, which lowers energy costs and protects the economy from rising oil prices. Cheap energy gives energy-intensive industries, such as aluminium smelting, a competitive edge. Greenhouses heated by geothermal energy grow vegetables and flowers all year, reducing food imports.

There are environmental benefits too. Geothermal energy is renewable and clean. It has cut Iceland's CO2 emissions by up to 37%, giving cleaner air. Geothermal pools and spas, such as the Blue Lagoon, attract tourists and improve wellbeing.

Interaction 2 - living with active rock processes: building power plants on active volcanic ground is risky. The Svartsengi geothermal plant needs lava barriers and protective dykes. The 2023-2024 Grindavik eruptions destroyed houses and forced the rebuilding of roads and bridges. Monitoring and emergency planning add ongoing costs.

The Philippines also uses hot rocks under volcanoes such as Mayon. It ranks third in the world for geothermal electricity, cutting fuel imports.

Diagram: magma chamber heating rock; water pumped down; steam rising to a power station.

prompt:
Urban Development
Examine how two of the following factors have influenced the development of any urban area that you have studied:
- Transport
- Location
- Primary economic activity.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Urban area: Galway City.

Factor 1: Location.
Influence: Galway's location on the River Corrib, where it meets Galway Bay, made it a trading port.
In 1232 the Anglo-Normans built a castle here, at today's Druid Lane, because the river gave defence and access to the sea. Galway grew into a walled trading town. Taxes on traded goods paid for the walls, which had five gates with tolls. From about 1400 fourteen merchant families, the 'Tribes of Galway', grew wealthy through sea trade, so commerce became the main function. Around 1750 the Eyre family built a quay and dock at the Long Walk, adding a port function. The river also powered grain mills and supplied distilleries and breweries in the 1800s, giving the city an industrial function. Its coastal location later let Salthill grow as a seaside resort.

Factor 2: Transport.
Influence: improved transport links turned Galway into a tourist, industrial and university city.
In 1851 the railway from Dublin arrived, along with the Railway Hotel (now the Hardiman). This began Galway's tourist function, and visitors flocked to Salthill. Tourism grew further after Shannon Airport opened in the 1960s, and Knock Airport later added more access. The M6 motorway to Dublin and the M18 make the city easy to reach for visitors and businesses. Good communications helped attract multinationals. Galway's first industrial estate opened at Mervue in 1967. Today Boston Scientific, Medtronic and others locate here, using the M6, the rail link and access to Dublin Port and Airport to export products. As a result, Galway is now a multifunctional city with strong commerce, industry, education and tourism.

prompt:
Primary Economic Activity
Explain any two factors that have influenced the development of one primary economic activity in an Irish region that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Activity: agriculture in the West of Ireland (Donegal, Mayo, Galway).

Factor 1: Climate.
The West faces the Atlantic and gets prevailing south-westerly winds full of moisture. When this air rises over the western mountains it cools and condenses, giving heavy relief rainfall of about 1,600 mm a year, almost twice the East. This heavy rain causes leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease, which limit cereal growing. Less than 2% of Ireland's cereals were grown in the West in 2023. More cloud also gives a shorter growing season than the East, which has about 280 days. The wet climate does suit grass, so farming is mainly pastoral. Most farms keep sheep and dry stock cattle (fattened for beef), which earn less than dairying or tillage. Over 20% of Ireland's grassland is in the West.

Factor 2: Soils (and relief).
The West has mostly infertile soils. Glacial erosion in the last Ice Age stripped soil from the uplands, leaving rocky ground. Very high rainfall formed acidic, waterlogged peat soils on the uplands of west Donegal, west Mayo and west Galway. Granite in west Galway weathers into poor clay soils that are unsuitable for tillage. In east Mayo, podzols are badly leached, and hard pans around Ballyhaunis cause waterlogging and low yields. Steep slopes, such as around Croagh Patrick, make machinery hard to use. As a result farms are small, averaging 25.5 hectares compared with 32.5 hectares nationally. Teagasc says almost two-thirds of western farms are not economically viable, and over half of western farmers work part-time.

prompt:
The European Union
Discuss the potential challenges facing the future development of the European Union with reference to factors such as political union, economic union and sovereignty.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Challenge 1: Tax harmony and sovereignty (economic union).
The EU wants fiscal union - one central tax system for income tax, VAT and corporation tax. Supporters say it would control government spending and bring stability. Opponents, including Ireland, say larger countries like France and Germany would gain an unfair advantage. Ireland's success depends on US multinationals such as Google, Apple and Pfizer, attracted by a 15% corporation tax. Many also fear losing sovereignty, the ability to govern themselves, because decisions would be made by an unelected body. In 2016 the EU ordered Apple to pay EUR 13 billion in back taxes to Ireland, and the Irish government opposed the EU in the case. This tension could slow deeper economic union.

Challenge 2: Brexit (economic union).
The UK voted to leave in 2016 and left on 31 January 2020. The EU lost a wealthy market of 60 million people. Tariffs and customs checks raised costs for businesses and consumers. Experts estimate Brexit costs the EU EUR 12 billion a year in lost trade. It also showed that member states can leave, which could encourage other exits.

Challenge 3: Security and political union.
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 restarted debate on a common security policy or even an EU army. Neutral countries such as Ireland do not want to lose neutrality. Hungary under Viktor Orban refused to condemn Russia, showing how hard it is to agree.

A further challenge is immigration and the rise of the far right. Parties such as National Rally in France and AfD in Germany blame migrants for social pressures, threatening the EU's values of democracy and human rights.

prompt:
Population in Ireland
Account for the distribution of population throughout an Irish region that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Region: the West of Ireland (Galway, Mayo and Donegal).

Population in the West is uneven. It is sparse in the uplands and on the Atlantic fringe, and clustered in towns, coastal lowlands and river valleys.

Physical landscape: the West has rugged mountains such as the Twelve Pins and the Nephin Beg Range. Steep slopes, harsh weather and poor, wet peat soils make farming and building difficult, so densities are very low. Areas above 500 m are colder and hard to reach. People cluster instead on lowlands, such as east Galway, where brown earth soils support dairying.

Resources and jobs: the West lacks resources and industrial jobs, so densities are low. Farms are small and many are not viable. Young people leave for jobs in towns and cities, so rural populations shrink and age. Moygownagh, Co. Mayo, has lost 90% of its population since 1841.

Urban centres: population is highest in Galway City, which has a university, hospitals and multinationals such as Boston Scientific (over 4,000 jobs). It attracts migrants and is projected to grow 40% to about 86,000 by 2040. Towns at river crossings, such as Ballina on the Moy, are nodal points with higher densities.

Health and services: Mayo and Donegal have fewer health facilities, despite ageing populations. Only 10% of Irish GPs work in rural areas, which pushes young families towards Galway City.

Culture and language: after the 1950s Irish was mainly spoken in Gaeltacht areas. A lack of jobs led young people to leave, so areas such as Connemara declined.

History: during the Great Famine (1845-1852) death and emigration caused rural populations to fall drastically. Rural decline continued for more than a century and is still seen in remote western areas.

prompt:
Mobility of Economic Activities
Examine the mobility of modern economic activities with reference to one multinational company that you have studied.

model_answer:
MNC: Boston Scientific.

Boston Scientific is an American MedTech company with its headquarters in Marlborough, Massachusetts. It makes heart stents, valves, pacemakers and other devices. Like many modern firms it is footloose: it can move easily from place to place, so it locates where conditions give it the greatest advantage. It has branch plants in 40 countries on six continents and over 53,000 employees.

In 1994 it opened its first and largest Irish plant at Ballybrit, Galway. It also has plants in Clonmel, Co. Tipperary and Cork City. It employs over 4,000 people in Galway.

Mobility is shaped by tax policy. Governments compete to attract mobile companies. Ireland's low corporation tax, 12.5% from 1997 and now 15%, plus grants from IDA Ireland, drew the company here.

Mobility is shaped by labour. Galway is a MedTech cluster with Medtronic and smaller firms. The University of Galway and ATU Galway supply graduates in engineering and life sciences. The English-speaking workforce makes it easy to work with US managers.

Mobility is shaped by markets. Ireland is a gateway to the EU, giving tariff-free access to over 450 million people. Galway serves Europe, the Middle East and Africa and exports over 4 million devices a year using the M6 motorway, Dublin Port and Dublin Airport.

Research is also mobile. MNCs now spread R&D to wherever expertise exists - distributed innovation. Galway does design and R&D as well as manufacturing. Investment keeps flowing: a EUR 100 million expansion in 2022 created 300+ jobs, and EUR 75 million for cardiovascular R&D followed in 2026. Raw materials such as copper and ethylene oxide come from many places, so good transport is vital.

prompt:
Environmental Impact
Examine how economic activities can have an environmental impact with reference to examples on a local scale and a global scale.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Local scale - Impact: water pollution from intensive farming in Ireland.
Intensive dairy and beef farming uses large amounts of slurry and nitrogen fertiliser. After heavy rain, nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates run off fields into streams, rivers and lakes. This pollutes the water and harms fish and other aquatic life. Runoff of pesticides and animal waste also threatens human health. Heavy rain can cause soil erosion, washing nutrients away. Government schemes such as ACRES now pay farmers to protect water quality and biodiversity, and organic farms avoid artificial chemicals.

Local scale - second impact: tourism in Barcelona, Spain.
Mass tourism strains the local environment. Tourists in Catalonia use three times more water per day than residents. Bins on La Rambla are emptied up to 14 times a day. Cruise ships pollute the air: one emits as much nitrogen oxide as 30,000 cars a day. Anchoring boats damage Posidonia seagrass, which stores carbon and prevents coastal erosion. On the positive side, Catalonia spends over EUR 5 million a year of tourism taxes restoring coastal habitats.

Global scale - Impact: global warming from burning fossil fuels.
Industry, transport and power stations burn coal, oil and gas, releasing greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide. Agriculture adds methane from livestock; it is almost 20% of global emissions and over 40% in Ireland. These gases trap heat. In 2024 global temperatures rose 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels for the first time. As a result, Greenland's ice is melting at 200-270 gigatons a year, raising sea levels by about 2 mm a year. Melting permafrost could release even more carbon and methane, creating a feedback loop of further warming.

prompt:
Economic Development - Developed Economy
Examine the development of one of the following with reference to a developed economy that you have studied:
- Footloose industries
- Financial services
- Mass tourism.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Developed economy: Spain. Activity: mass tourism.

Mass tourism is the movement of large numbers of tourists to popular destinations. In Spain it grew from fewer than 1 million tourists in 1950 to a record 94 million in 2024.

Climate: the Mediterranean climate on the south and east coasts gives long, hot, dry summers of about 28 degrees C in July and over 300 days of sunshine. This dependable 'sun and sea' appeal attracts northern Europeans. Mild winters of 15-18 degrees C now also attract winter-sun visitors.

Rising incomes and leisure: after World War II, people in northern Europe had more disposable income. New labour laws gave paid holidays. Jumbo jets and cheaper travel, along with package holidays that bundled flights, hotels and activities, made Spain affordable.

Government marketing and investment: the Spanish Ministry of Tourism used tourism to rebuild the economy with its 'Spain is Different' campaign. It invested in airports such as Malaga, motorways, high-speed rail and water and sewerage in resorts. Hotels and resorts spread along the coast from the Costa Brava to the Costa del Sol. Torremolinos grew from a small fishing village into one of the busiest resorts. By the 1970s over 30 million tourists came each year.

Importance today: in 2024 tourism employed nearly 3 million people and was worth EUR 249 billion, 15% of GDP. A new hotel opened every four days.

Problems: development has also brought overcrowding, water shortages and rising rents. Short-term lets push locals out of Barcelona, leading to protests in 2024, and the city plans to stop renewing tourist apartment licences by 2029. Many jobs are low-paid and seasonal.

prompt:
Colonialism
Examine the impact of colonialism on a developing economy that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Developing economy: India.

Colonialism is when a powerful country takes control of another country to gain wealth, resources or power, imposing its own government, language and culture. Britain ruled 'British India' until 1947.

Impact 1: Partition, displacement and death.
When Britain granted independence in 1947, it divided British India along religious lines into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan. Pakistan was in two parts; East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971. The new borders left Muslim minorities in India and Hindu minorities in Pakistan, causing riots. About 12 million people fled Pakistan for India and over 10 million went the other way. About 1 million people died in violent clashes, leaving lasting bitterness. Such huge movements of people disrupted farming, trade and families.

Impact 2: The Kashmir conflict.
Under the rules for independence, local leaders chose which country to join. Kashmir's ruler, Maharaja Hari Singh, joined India even though 80% of the people were Muslims who wanted to join Pakistan. War broke out, and in 1949 a ceasefire line, the Line of Control, divided the region. There have been wars in 1965 and 1999 and many attacks since, such as Pulwama in 2019 and Pahalgam in 2025. Both countries are nuclear powers. Money is spent on the military instead of development. In Kashmir, violence causes tourism to collapse, damages water and electricity supplies and brings fear and repression. Pakistan also fears India's control of the source of the River Indus, a vital water supply.

Impact 3: Migration links.
Colonial ties still shape migration routes. As members of the Commonwealth, many people from India moved to Britain. India now has the world's largest diaspora, nearly 18 million people, who send home remittances.

prompt:
Renewable Energy
Examine how the development of renewable energy is crucial for Ireland's environment and economy.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Renewable energy comes from sources that do not run out, such as wind, solar, hydroelectric and geothermal power.

Environment - importance: renewables cut the greenhouse gas emissions that are causing climate change.
About four-fifths of human-induced warming comes from burning fossil fuels. In 2024 global temperatures rose 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels for the first time. Ireland is very exposed. About 40% of the population lives within 5 km of the coast, and 200 km2 of land in the Republic is at risk from rising seas, especially in Galway, Kerry, Cork and Dublin. Storms such as Eowyn in 2025 are becoming more severe. Under the Paris Agreement, Ireland must help keep warming well below 2 degrees C and aim for net zero. Switching to wind and solar power is the main way to cut emissions from electricity and transport, alongside electric cars and buses. Cleaner energy also means cleaner air and better health.

Economy - importance: renewables protect Ireland from high and unstable fossil fuel prices.
Ireland imports oil and gas. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, loss of Russian gas raised electricity and transport costs and the cost of living. In 2026 the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent oil prices up sharply. Home-grown renewable power gives energy security. Iceland shows the benefit: geothermal energy has cut fuel imports and energy costs.

Renewables also save money and attract investment. Ireland's carbon tax is EUR 63.50 per tonne of CO2 from petrol and diesel, so using less fossil fuel saves households and firms money. Government grants support solar panels and insulation. Multinationals want clean power: Boston Scientific's 2022 Galway expansion is powered by renewable energy. In the Gaeltacht, Udaras na Gaeltachta's An Ghaeltacht Ghlas helps business parks switch to renewable energy.

source: 2023 State Exam - Section 3 (Electives), Q9 C

prompt:
Urban Issues
Discuss any two of the following issues that may arise from the growth of urban settlements:
- Urban decay and absence of community
- Urban sprawl
- Environmental issues.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Example: Dublin.

Issue 1: Urban sprawl.
Urban sprawl is the spread of a city into rural land in a low-density, unplanned way. Dublin grew outwards in low-rise housing, reaching into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow to form the Greater Dublin Area. Causes include rapid population growth since the 1970s, the rezoning of farmland on the fringe, a preference for owning single-family homes, and high prices pushing people outwards. Many councils share planning, so it is poorly coordinated.
Sprawl brings long commutes. Public transport has not kept up, so car use rises and routes such as the M50 are badly congested. The average Irish commute was 29.1 minutes in 2022, double the EU average, and many commute over an hour. Fertile farmland in Meath and Kildare is lost to housing and retail parks. Hedgerows, woodland and wetlands are destroyed, harming red squirrels, badgers and pollinators. Car emissions and waste also increase.

Issue 2: Urban decay and absence of community.
Urban decay is when an area declines socially, economically and in population, leaving run-down and derelict buildings. In Dublin, businesses moved out to cheaper greenfield sites in the suburbs. Schools, shops and post offices closed. Those left behind were often older, poorer or less educated. This led to a loss of community spirit, alienation and anti-social behaviour such as vandalism, drugs and crime. Examples include O'Connell Street Upper and Parnell Street. Ballymun's tower blocks, built in the 1960s, had no shops, playgrounds or community centre and became known for decay. Sprawl also weakens community: long commutes leave people with little time for clubs, causing social isolation. Regeneration projects such as Ballymun and Smithfield aim to rebuild these communities.

- Question is not tied to Ireland.

prompt:
Migration
Describe and explain changes in patterns of migration to and from Ireland since 1950.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Change from Ireland: heavy emigration in the 1950s and 1980s has turned into lower, more skilled emigration today.
Change to Ireland: Ireland has changed from a country people left into a major destination for immigrants.

1950s: Ireland's population was only about 2.9 million. High unemployment forced thousands to emigrate, mainly to London, Liverpool and Manchester. Shared language and colonial links made Britain the main destination.

1960s-1970s: the government attracted multinationals and foreign investment. New jobs reduced emigration, and the population grew for the first time in over 120 years. Joining the EEC in 1973 brought larger markets and higher incomes, attracting migrants and encouraging people to stay.

1980s: a recession and high unemployment caused over 200,000 mainly young adults to emigrate to Britain, the US, Canada and Australia - a brain drain.

1995-2008 Celtic Tiger: rapid economic growth created jobs. Irish emigrants returned with new skills (brain gain), and workers came from the EU. After Poland joined the EU in 2004, many young Poles came for higher wages. In 2007 Polish workers sent over EUR 1.2 billion home.

After 2008: the financial crash caused renewed emigration of young adults. By 2010 almost 30,000 more people left than arrived.

Today: immigration is the main driver of population growth. People come from the EU, India and elsewhere to fill skills shortages, and almost 120,000 Ukrainians arrived after Russia's 2022 invasion. In the year to April 2024, the population rose by nearly 99,000. Emigration still continues, rising from 54,000 in 2021 to 65,600 in 2024, with young professionals going to Australia and Dubai for better pay and conditions.

prompt:
Dynamics of Population
Examine the impact of any one of the following factors on levels of population change, with reference to example(s) that you have studied:
- The development of resources
- Income levels
- Technology.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Factor: the development of resources.

Impact 1: developing resources creates jobs, which attracts migrants and increases population.
Natural resources such as water, fertile soil, minerals and fossil fuels give jobs and support larger populations. Khetri in Rajasthan, India, has one of India's largest copper mines. Its population grew about 50% in about 20 years, from 17,377 in 2001 to 26,400 in 2025. In Odisha, coal and iron ore support mining and an iron and steel industry. In West Bengal, jute grown on the Ganges Delta supports a labour-intensive textile industry that attracts migrants, giving very high densities.

In Ireland, Navan, Co. Meath, grew because of Tara Mines, Europe's largest lead and zinc mine. The Kinsale Head Gas Field powered Cork's industries, helping Cork become the second-largest city.

Impact 2: developing food resources lowers death rates and increases natural increase.
India's Green Revolution in the 1960s used irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides and high-yielding crops. Wheat output in Punjab rose from about 1 million tonnes in 1950 to over 10 million tonnes by 1985. There were fewer deaths from hunger, more children survived and life expectancy rose, so the population grew. Bihar benefited less, suffered food shortages and lost people through rural-to-urban migration.

Negative impact: a lack of developed resources causes population decline.
The west and northwest of Ireland lack resources and industrial jobs. Young people leave for jobs elsewhere, so rural populations fall and age. Moygownagh, Co. Mayo, has lost 90% of its population since 1841, closing its shop, pub and post office.

13. Empowering people is a way of linking economic growth with human development. Discuss this statement with reference to any two of the following:
- Aid programmes
- Land ownership patterns
- Differing gender roles in society.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: empowering people means giving them the skills, resources and power to make decisions about their own lives. This essay discusses aid programmes and differing gender roles, using Irish Aid in Ethiopia and examples from India.

Aspect 1: Long-term aid programmes that build local ownership.
Irish Aid is Ireland's overseas development programme. It works in over 130 countries and aims for long-term solutions, not just emergency help. Its 'A Better World' policy focuses on 'reaching the furthest behind first'. Irish Aid uses a partnership approach: it works with local governments, communities, NGOs and UN agencies so that aid fits local needs and is managed locally. In Ethiopia, which was the top recipient of Irish bilateral aid in 2024, Irish Aid funds the Civil Society Support Programme. Communities identify their own needs and propose improvements. It also trains teachers and local leaders so that programmes continue after Irish Aid leaves. This empowers communities to lead change and become less dependent on aid, linking human development with lasting economic growth.

Aspect 2: Aid that improves food security and incomes.
Ethiopia lies on the edge of the Sahara and suffers drought, desertification and famine. Irish Aid supports Ethiopian researchers and farmers to grow more food in a difficult climate. Farmers use drought-resistant crops such as potatoes and agroforestry, where trees are planted alongside crops to protect soil and hold moisture. In Tigray, water tanks, irrigation channels and small dams store rainfall, and some farmers increased harvests by up to 30% even in low rainfall. Irish Aid also supports small dairy farmers to improve methods and output. Higher yields give farmers more income to spend on education and health, so economic growth and human development rise together. In emergencies, cash assistance lets people buy essentials while also supporting local markets.

Aspect 3: Changing gender roles - empowering women.
In many societies women have had less access to education, work and money. Irish Aid helps Ethiopian women set up small businesses by giving training, access to credit and livestock. This gives women skills, confidence, income and independence, and improves household security. It supports SDG 5, gender equality. In the Afar region, Irish Aid supports an initiative to tackle female genital mutilation and child marriage, protecting girls' rights to health and education. Investment in health is also empowering: between 2020 and 2025, births with a midwife present rose from 18% to 28%, and infant mortality fell. School feeding keeps children healthy and in school.

Aspect 4: Gender equality, smaller families and economic growth in India.
India shows how empowering women links growth and development. In Kerala, female literacy is 97% and the fertility rate is 1.7. More girls finish school and more women work, so families are smaller and living standards are higher. In contrast, in Bihar female literacy is as low as 60% and early marriage gives a fertility rate of 3.0, double Kerala's. India's 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao' campaign (2015) promotes girls' education and challenges 'son preference'. Empowered women have fewer children and invest more in each child, which lowers infant mortality, raises life expectancy and strengthens the economy.

Conclusion: when aid is locally owned and when women gain equal access to education, work and money, people become active drivers of development. Economic growth then goes hand in hand with better health, education and wellbeing.

prompt:
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
14. Views of development and underdevelopment involve contrasting models and approaches to development.
Discuss.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: countries try to develop in different ways. Three contrasting approaches are protectionism, modernisation and sustainable development. Each sees development differently, and how we measure development also shapes our view of it.

Aspect 1: Protectionism - development by protecting home industry.
Protectionism is when a government restricts international trade. It uses tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the amount imported) and subsidies (government support for local firms). These make imports dearer, so consumers buy local goods and domestic industries grow. The United States is an example. Import tariffs make goods from China and Europe more expensive, and tariffs on steel imports encouraged people to buy US-made steel. In April 2025 Donald Trump imposed tariffs on many countries, with the highest on China. In the short term this protects jobs and home-grown industry. In the long term consumers may pay more and the economy may become less efficient. Other countries retaliate with their own tariffs, leading to trade wars, and global trade becomes less stable.

Aspect 2: Modernisation - development in stages by copying richer countries.
Modernisation theory says that if less economically developed countries copy more developed ones - investing in modern technology, industry and education - they will grow wealthier. Development happens in stages: traditional farming societies adopt new ideas, become more urban and build industry. China is an example. It changed from a rural, farming country to a world leader in technology and industry, investing heavily in robotics and engineering. Jobs caused huge rural-to-urban migration, e.g. to Shenzhen. Many people were lifted out of poverty. However, critics say every country is unique and this path does not suit all. China now has inequality between poorer rural and richer urban areas, and environmental pressure. Beijing went from 77,000 cars in 1978 to millions by 2018, showing the shift to cars as it modernised.

Aspect 3: Sustainable development - balancing people, planet and economy.
Sustainable development aims to solve problems such as hunger, poverty and pollution without harming the ability of future generations to meet their needs. It has three linked pillars: environmental (clean air, water, forests), economic (jobs, a stable economy) and social (fairness and reducing poverty). The UN Sustainable Development Goals set worldwide targets. Finland ranked first on the 2025 SDG Index. It balances growth with environmental protection and social fairness, prioritising recycling, clean transport, health and education, and aims to be carbon neutral by 2035. This approach benefits people and nature, but it is slow and the pillars are hard to balance.

Aspect 4: Contrasting ways of measuring development.
Views of development also depend on how it is measured. GDP measures the value of goods and services produced, but it ignores inequality, health and the environment. The Human Development Index adds life expectancy, education and income. Ireland's HDI is 0.949, ranked 11th, while Afghanistan's is 0.462, ranked 182nd. This shows differences in daily life, not just wealth. The Gender Development Index shows gaps between men and women. No single measure is perfect, so several should be used together.

Conclusion: there is no single route out of underdevelopment. Leaders must choose an approach that fits their country's wealth, resources and problems.

prompt:
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
15. We live in an interdependent global economy. Discuss the impact of social and political decisions with reference to each of the following:
- Economic and political refugees
- Migration patterns
- Human rights issues.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: decisions made by governments and societies in one country affect people all over the world. They can force people to flee, open or close migration routes, and protect or deny human rights.

Aspect 1: Political decisions create political refugees.
A refugee is a person forced to flee their country because of persecution, conflict or violence. The decision by Russia to invade Ukraine in February 2022 caused one of the largest refugee crises in recent history. Over 6.8 million refugees fled Ukraine, about 92% to other European countries, and about 8 million more were displaced inside Ukraine. About 90% of those who left were women and children, because men aged 18-60 had to stay for military service. The EU's political decision to give Temporary Protection let Ukrainians live, work and study in member states. Almost 120,000 came to Ireland. Similarly, in Sudan the civil war between two military groups since 2023 has forced up to 14 million people from their homes, with over 4 million in crowded camps in neighbouring countries.

Aspect 2: Economic decisions and economic refugees.
Economic migrants leave because of poverty and lack of jobs. In Sub-Saharan Africa extreme poverty and high youth unemployment push young people to Europe and North America to earn money and send remittances home. In the Sahel, drought and desertification destroy farming. Political decisions shape what happens next: 'climate refugee' is not recognised under the 1951 Refugee Convention, so people displaced by climate disasters have no legal protection. Decisions by wealthy, high-emitting countries on climate action also affect how many people will be forced to move.

Aspect 3: Government policy changes migration patterns.
Political decisions open and close migration routes. After World War II, Britain invited workers from the Caribbean and other Commonwealth countries. Over 500,000 arrived between 1948 and 1971, the Windrush generation, with no visas needed. When Poland joined the EU in 2004, free movement allowed many young Poles to come to Ireland for higher wages. Ireland's Critical Skills Employment Permit now attracts skilled workers from outside Europe to fill shortages in healthcare, engineering and IT. The EU Migration and Asylum Pact requires refugees to apply for asylum in the first EU country they enter, and Ireland's International Protection Bill (2025) aims to make the asylum system faster.

Aspect 4: Human rights issues.
Decisions can deny human rights. In the Windrush Scandal, many Caribbean migrants who had lived in Britain for decades had never been given official papers. Some lost jobs, could not access healthcare, and some were deported. In Afghanistan, Taliban policies closed girls' secondary schools and restricted women's education and work. Migrants also face racism: Ireland had 600 reports of racism in 2022, and anti-immigration riots in Dublin in 2024. Far-right parties in Europe blame migrants, threatening the EU's values of human dignity, equality and human rights. Positive decisions, such as the Schools of Sanctuary programme and Failte Isteach English classes, help protect the rights and integration of migrants.

Conclusion: in an interdependent world, social and political decisions in one place shape the lives, movement and rights of millions elsewhere.

16. Soil characteristics are affected by a combination of soil processes operating in their immediate environment. Examine how any three of the following processes impact on soil characteristics:
- Weathering
- Soil erosion
- Leaching
- Podzolisation.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: soil is made of mineral matter, organic matter (humus), air and water. Processes such as weathering, leaching and podzolisation, controlled by Ireland's climate and vegetation, give each soil its own colour, texture, drainage and fertility.

Aspect 1: Weathering - creating the mineral content and texture of soil.
Weathering breaks down rock into smaller pieces at the Earth's surface. This parent material gives soil its minerals and texture. Mechanical weathering, such as freeze-thaw, breaks rock apart: water in cracks freezes, expands by about 9% and shatters the rock, producing coarse fragments. Chemical weathering changes the minerals. Carbonation dissolves calcium carbonate in limestone and carries it away in solution. Oxidation turns iron in rock into reddish iron oxide, giving some soils and sandstones a rusty colour. The type of rock matters: granite in west Galway weathers into poor clay soils that are unsuitable for tillage. In contrast, the brown earths of the east and south developed on glacial deposits about 10,000 years old. These contain a variety of minerals, giving a loamy texture - a balance of sand, silt and clay - which is well-drained and well-aerated. In soil profiles, the weathered parent material forms the lowest layer.

Aspect 2: Leaching - washing nutrients down the profile.
Leaching is when rainwater percolating through the soil washes nutrients down into the lower horizons. Its strength depends on rainfall. The west of Ireland gets about 1,600 mm a year from relief rainfall, almost twice the east (about 800 mm). In the wetter west, heavy leaching leaves the topsoil short of nutrients and more acidic, lowering fertility. This limits cereal growing, so farming is mainly pastoral. In east Mayo, podzols are severely leached. In the drier east, such as Dublin with about 800 mm, there is little leaching. Brown earths there keep their nutrients near the surface, stay fertile and well-drained, and are ideal for arable farming. Leaching can also move iron down the profile: in waterlogged gley soils, iron turns bluish-grey and is leached downwards.

Aspect 3: Podzolisation - forming infertile podzols with an iron pan.
Podzolisation is an extreme form of leaching. It happens in areas of heavy rainfall under coniferous forest, e.g. Counties Cork and Cavan. Conifer needles give poor plant litter, which forms a raw, acidic humus (mor). The acidic water percolating down removes nutrients, iron and organic matter from the upper layers. This leaves a pale, ash-grey layer near the top. The iron and organic matter build up lower down to form a hard iron pan (hardpan). The iron pan blocks drainage, so the soil above becomes waterlogged. The soil is acidic, so there is little microbial action, which slows decomposition further. The result is an infertile, poorly drained soil. Around Ballyhaunis, hard pans cause waterlogging and low tillage yields. A podzol profile shows: needles and cones; raw acid humus; ash-grey layer; iron pan; reddish-brown layer; parent material.

Conclusion: weathering supplies the raw material, while climate-driven leaching and podzolisation decide whether a soil ends up fertile like brown earth or infertile like a podzol.

prompt:

17. Biomes are altered by human activities. Discuss.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: a biome is a large natural region with its own climate, plants, animals and soils. Ireland's biome is the temperate deciduous rainforest. Human activities such as clearing forests, farming, draining bogs, building and burning fossil fuels have greatly changed it.

Aspect 1: Deforestation and the loss of native woodland.
Before humans, broadleaf deciduous forests of oak, ash, alder, birch and hazel covered much of Ireland. These woods had layers: a canopy, an understorey of hazel and holly, a field layer of bluebells and ferns, and a ground layer of mosses. Centuries of clearance for farming have taken Ireland from one of the most forested to one of the least forested countries in Europe. Only 10% of Ireland is now woodland, and only one-fifth of that is native. Many commercial forests are fast-growing conifers such as Sitka spruce. Under conifers in areas of heavy rain, poor needle litter and leaching cause podzolisation, forming infertile, acidic podzols with an iron pan. Losing native woodland also removes habitats for species like the red squirrel and pine marten.

Aspect 2: Intensive farming.
The fertile brown earths of the east and south are now mainly farmland. Intensive dairy and beef farming uses slurry and nitrogen fertiliser. Nutrient runoff of nitrates and phosphates pollutes streams, rivers and lakes, harming aquatic life. Agriculture produces over 40% of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, much of it methane from livestock. Hedgerows, which act as wildlife corridors, have been lost in many areas. In 2025 the European Environment Agency said nature in Ireland is in 'a very poor state', with 85% of protected habitats having 'unfavourable status'. Schemes such as REPS, GLAS and ACRES now pay farmers to replant native hedges, protect nesting birds and reduce runoff.

Aspect 3: Draining and cutting peat bogs.
Peat bogs are intrazonal soils in the midlands and west. They hold over 90% water and support rare plants such as bog cotton and bladderworts and invertebrates such as the raft spider. Ireland has 8% of the world's blanket bogs, which store millions of tonnes of carbon. When bogs are drained and reclaimed for pasture, they dry out and release carbon into the atmosphere, adding to climate change, and their unique habitats are lost. Today Bord na Mona is rehabilitating and rewetting peatlands to capture carbon, improve water quality and act as natural sponges that reduce flooding.

Aspect 4: Urban sprawl and climate change.
As Dublin sprawls into Meath and Kildare, fertile farmland, woodland, hedgerows and wetlands are replaced by houses and retail parks. This harms red squirrels, pine martens, hares and badgers, and pollinators lose food. Urban foxes now scavenge bins. Human-induced climate change also alters the biome. Warmer weather lets pests and diseases spread. Heavy rain destroys the nests of ground-nesting bees, and changing temperatures cause flowers to bloom when pollinators are not active (phenological mismatch). 30% of Ireland's 100 native bee species are at risk of extinction.

Conclusion: humans have greatly reduced Ireland's natural biome, but rewetting bogs, planting native trees and agri-environment schemes show that people can also help to restore it.

18. Describe and explain the general composition and characteristics of any one soil type.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: brown earth is the most common soil in Ireland. It is a zonal soil, formed mainly by climate and vegetation. It is found in the lowlands of the east and south, e.g. Co. Wexford and Co. Meath.

Aspect 1: Mineral matter, parent material and texture.
Brown earths developed on glacial deposits laid down about 10,000 years ago, at the end of the last Ice Age. Ice carried and mixed material from many rock types, so the soil contains a variety of minerals. Weathering of this parent material gives a loamy texture: a balanced mix of sand, silt and clay. The structure is granular, with rounded, grain-like crumbs. These spaces between crumbs let air and water move easily, so the soil is well-drained and well-aerated with good percolation. Deep roots take up minerals from the lower layers and return them to the surface in leaf fall.

Aspect 2: Organic matter, humus and soil organisms.
Brown earths formed under the deciduous forests of oak and ash that once covered the east and south. Each autumn these trees shed leaves, giving a rich supply of plant litter. Ireland's mild temperatures mean the ground rarely freezes, so earthworms, insects, fungi and bacteria are active for most of the year. They break down the litter rapidly into humus, a dark, jelly-like substance. This process gives a mild humus with plenty of plant food. Earthworms mix the humus with the mineral matter, so there are no sharp layers between horizons. High humus content makes the soil dark brown; this dark colour absorbs heat. Humus also holds water, so the soil does not waterlog in heavy rain and never fully dries out in dry spells.

Aspect 3: Climate, leaching and drainage.
The east and south are in the rain shadow of the western mountains. They receive about 800 mm of rain a year, compared with about 1,600 mm in the west. They are also slightly warmer and sunnier. With less rain, there is little leaching, so nutrients stay near the surface rather than being washed down. There is no bleached layer and no hardpan, unlike podzols. The soil remains well-drained and well-aerated.

Aspect 4: pH, profile and fertility.
The pH ranges from slightly alkaline to slightly acidic, depending on rainfall and parent material, which is ideal for microbes. The profile has leaf debris on top, then a mild acid humus layer, a dark brown A horizon, a merging boundary, a lighter brown B horizon, and weathered parent material at the base. Because they are deep, fertile, nutrient-rich and well-drained, brown earths are Ireland's best farming soils. They are ideal for arable farming, such as cereals and potatoes; Meath potatoes supply Tayto Snacks. They also support the most productive dairy and beef farms and the largest population centres.

Conclusion: the brown earth's mix of minerals, rich humus, active organisms and low leaching makes it the most fertile and useful soil in Ireland.

prompt:
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
22. Examine how solar energy is transformed and redistributed through circulation patterns in the atmosphere and oceans.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: the sun heats the Earth unequally. The atmosphere and oceans act like conveyor belts, moving heat from the hot tropics towards the cold poles. Without this, the equator would grow ever hotter and the poles ever colder.

Aspect 1: Unequal heating - why heat must be redistributed.
The equator is warmest because the sun's rays are concentrated on a small area and pass through a small amount of atmosphere, so little energy is lost. At the poles the rays arrive at a low angle, spread over a larger area and pass through more atmosphere, so they give little warmth. The Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5 degrees, so heating changes with the seasons. Ice and snow at the poles reflect up to 90% of sunlight (high albedo), keeping them cold. Solar energy is transformed when it is absorbed by the land and sea and radiated as heat to warm the air above. Most heat in the atmosphere radiates up from the surface, which is why temperature falls with height. This imbalance of energy drives the circulation of air and water. One function of the atmosphere is to transfer heat from the tropics towards the poles.

Aspect 2: Atmospheric circulation - the three-cell model.
At the equator, intense heat makes air rise, creating low pressure. The north-east and south-east trade winds meet here at the Intertropical Convergence Zone. Rising air cools and condenses, giving heavy convectional rain. The air then moves towards the poles at height. By 15-30 degrees N and S it is cooler and drier, so it sinks and spreads out, forming high pressure - the horse latitudes. This loop is the Hadley cell. Sinking air warms, so hot deserts such as the Sahara form here. Some air flows back to the equator as trade winds; some moves towards the poles as the westerlies, forming the mid-latitude cell. Near the poles, cold air sinks and flows outwards in the polar cell. Between 30 and 60 degrees, where warm moist tropical air moving north meets cold polar air moving south, mid-latitude cyclones form and carry this air across regions such as Ireland.

Aspect 3: Winds and air masses carry heat.
Winds redistribute heat around the world. Ireland's prevailing south-westerly wind blows from the Gulf of Mexico near the tropics, bringing warm air and a mild climate. Newfoundland, at a similar latitude, receives cold northerly winds from the North Pole, bringing ice and snow. Air masses take on the temperature of the area they form over. Tropical Maritime air from the Atlantic is warm and moist, while Polar Maritime air from Greenland is cold and showery. Sea air masses store heat and release it slowly in winter, moderating coastal temperatures. Land air masses heat and cool quickly: Samara in Russia, at the same latitude as Ireland, has a temperature range of 42 degrees C.

Aspect 4: Ocean currents - the ocean conveyor.
Ocean currents are part of a global conveyor system that moves heat, nutrients and salt. Warm currents flow away from the equator. The Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift carry warm tropical water north, warming the air above. Prevailing winds carry this warm air onto Ireland and north-west Europe, raising winter temperatures and keeping coasts ice-free. In the Atlantic, this system is the AMOC. Warm, less dense surface water flows north, cools and sinks near the Arctic, then cold deep water returns south. It moves nearly 20 million m3 of water per second, about 100 times the flow of the Amazon. Cold currents flow from the poles towards the equator, e.g. the Labrador Current and the Canaries Current, cooling the coasts they pass. Melting Greenland ice is diluting the Atlantic's salinity, and the AMOC is at its weakest in about 1,600 years.

Conclusion: atmospheric cells, winds, air masses and ocean currents work together to spread the sun's energy from the tropics to the poles, creating the world's climate zones.

prompt:
Note: It is better to discuss three or four aspects of the theme in some detail, rather than to give a superficial treatment of a large number of points.
23. Give an account of how atmosphere-ocean phenomena (e.g. pressure, temperature, wind and humidity) are measured and examine the importance of such measurements.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: meteorologists, such as those at Met Eireann, measure the atmosphere using instruments at weather stations, on buoys and ships, and from balloons, radar and satellites. These measurements are vital for forecasting, warnings and understanding climate change.

Aspect 1: Measuring pressure and temperature.
Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by the weight of air above a point. It is measured with a barometer in millibars or hectopascals. Inside an aneroid barometer, a flexible metal box expands or contracts as pressure changes, moving a pointer on a dial. Readings are used to draw isobars - lines joining places of equal pressure - at 4 hPa intervals on synoptic charts. Low pressure, marked L, brings wet, windy weather; high pressure, marked H, brings calm, settled weather. Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius with a maximum-minimum thermometer, which contains alcohol and mercury. Small metal markers in the tubes record the highest and lowest temperatures reached. Temperatures can be shown as isotherms, lines joining equal temperature.

Aspect 2: Measuring wind, humidity and precipitation.
Wind speed is measured with an anemometer in kilometres per hour: three cups rotate faster in stronger winds and a meter counts the rotations. Wind direction is shown by a wind vane, whose arrow points to where the wind blows from. Wind data can be shown on wind rose charts. Relative humidity is measured with a hygrometer as a percentage; saturated air is 100%. It has a dry bulb and a wet bulb thermometer, kept wet by muslin dipped in water. Humidity is worked out from the difference between them. Rainfall is measured in millimetres with a rain gauge: a funnel directs rain into a measuring cylinder. Cloud cover is measured in oktas (eighths of the sky), and a ceilometer uses a laser to measure the height of the cloud base.

Aspect 3: Remote sensing of the atmosphere and oceans.
Weather balloons carry radiosondes, which measure temperature, humidity and pressure at different heights and transmit the data back. Doppler radar detects precipitation and wind speed and direction. Satellites give global coverage. The Copernicus satellites monitor atmospheric gases, ice-sheet melt and sea levels, and Sentinel-2 loops the world every 100 minutes. At sea, weather stations, buoys and research vessels collect local ocean and weather data.

Aspect 4: The importance of measurements.
Accurate data lets meteorologists produce synoptic charts and forecasts. Using these measurements, Met Eireann issued a status red warning before Storm Eowyn in January 2025. Its gusts reached 184 km/h at Mace Head, Co. Galway. Early warnings let people stay safe and protect property. The European Flood Awareness System and European Forest Fire Information System use measurements to warn of floods and wildfires. Long-term records show climate change: they show that global temperatures rose 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels in 2024, and that Greenland is losing 200-270 gigatons of ice a year. Under the Paris Agreement, every country must monitor and report its emissions. Data also help farmers plan, and help planners prepare for sea-level rise and storm surges.

Conclusion: measuring the atmosphere and oceans saves lives, protects property and the economy, and gives the evidence needed to tackle climate change.

24. Examine how climate characteristics influence economic development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Introduction: climate is the average weather of a region over 30 years or more. Temperature, rainfall and extreme weather affect farming, tourism, health and infrastructure, so they strongly influence how developed a country can become.

Aspect 1: A mild, wet climate supports productive farming in Ireland.
Ireland has a cool temperate oceanic climate. Winters average about 6 degrees C and summers about 16 degrees C. Rain falls all year, with no dry season. This suits grass, so Ireland has a highly productive, export-driven dairy and beef sector, e.g. in the Golden Vale of Munster. Agriculture is worth about 8% of GDP, a record EUR 17 billion in 2024, and employs almost 10% of the workforce. Ireland produced 603,000 tonnes of beef in 2024, 90% of it exported. The drier east, at about 800 mm of rain a year, has less leaching and a growing season of 280 days, so it supports tillage and larger, more profitable farms. These farming exports help explain Ireland's high HDI of 0.949.

Aspect 2: A wetter climate limits development in the West of Ireland.
The West gets about 1,600 mm of rain a year from relief rainfall. This causes leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease, which limit cereals; less than 2% of Irish cereals were grown in the West in 2023. Farming is mainly less profitable sheep and dry stock. Farms are small, and Teagasc says almost two-thirds are not economically viable. Young people leave, leaving a poorer, ageing region. This shows how climate can help create peripheral regions.

Aspect 3: A sunny climate drives tourism in Spain.
Spain's Mediterranean coasts have long, hot, dry summers of about 28 degrees C in July and over 300 days of sunshine. This dependable 'sun and sea' climate made Spain a mass tourism destination. Tourist numbers rose from fewer than 1 million in 1950 to a record 94 million in 2024. Tourism employs nearly 3 million people and was worth EUR 249 billion in 2024, 15% of GDP. However, climate can also threaten development: heatwaves of 35-40 degrees C reduce summer demand, and droughts and wildfires put pressure on water and infrastructure.

Aspect 4: A dry or extreme climate holds back developing countries.
Afghanistan has a dry climate with frequent droughts, unpredictable rain and extreme temperatures, with severe drought since 2021. About 80% of Afghans depend on farming, so drought means failed crops, food shortages and malnutrition. Soil erosion and desertification lower incomes. Up to 97% of Afghans live in poverty, and its HDI is among the lowest in the world. In Malawi, Cyclone Freddy in 2023 dropped six months of rain in six days. The crops and livestock of over 2 million farmers were wiped out and 659,000 people were displaced. Cereal production fell 10.8% between 2023 and 2024. Such disasters raise food prices, increase poverty and reduce export earnings.

Conclusion: a favourable climate can be a major economic advantage, but extreme or unreliable climates make development much harder - and climate change is increasing these risks.

prompt:
1B. Human Interaction with Surface Processes
Human activity impacts on surface processes.
Examine this statement with reference to one of the following:
- The impact of flood control measures on river processes
- The impact of coastal defence measures on coastal processes
- The impact of human activities on mass movement processes.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Flood control measures change how a river erodes, transports and deposits its load.

Impact 1: Flood control increases the river's capacity to carry water and reduces flooding. In November 2009 the Clare River burst its banks at Claregalway, Co. Galway, after weeks of heavy rain on saturated ground. The OPW and Galway County Council built a flood relief scheme, completed in 2019 at a cost of EUR 11.4 million, protecting 77 properties. Extra arches called flood eyes were added to Claregalway Bridge and Crusheeney Bridge. Bridges are pinch-points where water backs up, so the flood eyes raise their hydraulic capacity and let floodwater pass through quickly. The river no longer spills onto its floodplain so often, so less alluvium is deposited there.

Impact 2: Dredging changes the channel. The channel was deepened and widened upstream and downstream of Claregalway Bridge. A deeper, wider channel improves conveyance, so water flows more efficiently. This means the river keeps its energy and carries its load further downstream instead of depositing it.

Impact 3: Embankments and flood walls keep water in the channel. They stop the river reaching its natural floodplain, which normally acts as a safety valve, slowing floodwater and reducing erosion damage.

Impact 4: Nature-based measures reduce surface run-off. In Crumlin Village, Dublin, SuDS such as filter drains, tree pits and filtration zones let rainwater soak into the ground. Much less surface water reaches the River Camac, so peak discharge falls, the river has less energy to erode, and pollutants are filtered out.

prompt:
1C. Destructive Plate Boundaries
Discuss the impacts of destructive plate boundaries, with reference to an example(s) you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
At a destructive (convergent) boundary two plates collide. Slab pull drags the denser plate down into the mantle.

Impact 1: Deep ocean trenches and volcanoes. Where the oceanic Nazca Plate meets the continental South American Plate, the Nazca Plate is subducted, forming the Peru-Chile Trench. As the sinking plate heats up, water is released, which lowers the melting point of the mantle. Magma forms, rises through the crust and erupts. Repeated eruptions build a chain of volcanoes parallel to the trench, the Andes volcanic arc. The lava is acidic, so eruptions are explosive and form steep stratovolcanoes.

Impact 2: Fold mountains. The sinking plate scrapes and compresses the edge of the continent, so the crust thickens, folds and is pushed up, forming the Andes. Where two continental plates collide there is little subduction, so rocks buckle into anticlines and synclines, e.g. the Alps (African and Eurasian Plates).

Impact 3: Powerful earthquakes. Stress builds up as the plates grind together and is released suddenly. The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile (magnitude 9.5) was the largest ever recorded. It made about 2 million people homeless and killed over 1,600 people in Chile.

Impact 4: Island arcs and tsunamis. Near Japan the denser Pacific Plate is subducted under the Eurasian Plate, forming the Japan Trench and a chain of volcanic islands (an island arc). Sea-floor earthquakes here can trigger tsunamis that devastate low-lying coasts.

prompt:
2B. Landscape Development
(i) Examine the role of the processes of erosion on the formation of one fluvial landform or one coastal landform or one glacial landform that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Landform: a cirque (corrie), e.g. the Devil's Punch Bowl, Mangerton Mountain, Co. Kerry.
Processes of erosion: plucking and abrasion (helped by freeze-thaw).

A cirque is a bowl-shaped hollow, steep on three sides with a lip at the front. It is called the birthplace of the glacier.

During the Ice Age snow gathered in hollows high in the mountains, often on north-facing slopes, and was compressed into ice. Freeze-thaw action broke up the rock: water seeped into cracks, froze, expanded by about 9% and split the rock into scree. This continuous freezing, thawing and breaking is called nivation. It widened and deepened the hollow so more snow could collect.

When the ice reached about 50 m deep it began to move downslope, turning under its own weight in a rotational slip. Gaps called bergschrunds opened at the back of the ice.

Plucking: the weight of the ice melted some ice at its base. Meltwater seeped into joints in the back wall, refroze onto the rock and pulled pieces away as the glacier moved. This steepened the back wall.

Abrasion: plucked rocks and scree stuck in the base of the ice scraped the floor of the hollow like sandpaper, deepening it and leaving scratches called striations. Rotational slip meant abrasion was strongest at the back of the hollow, so the floor was over-deepened and a rock lip was left at the front.

After the Ice Age the ice melted and water filled the hollow, forming a tarn lake.

prompt:
2C. Volcanic Activity
Examine the influence of volcanic activity on the development of the Irish landscape with reference to each of the following:
- Intrusive features
- Extrusive features.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Intrusive feature: the Leinster Batholith.
A batholith forms when a huge mass of magma rises into the crust but does not reach the surface. About 400 million years ago the Eurasian and North American plates collided (Caledonian orogeny) and large amounts of magma formed. It was trapped deep underground and cooled very slowly, forming coarse-grained granite with large crystals. Heat from the magma baked the surrounding shale and sandstone into schist, slate and quartzite, a band of metamorphic rock. Over millions of years uplift, weathering and erosion stripped away the rock above, exposing the granite. The Leinster Batholith stretches over 120 km and forms the core of the Dublin-Wicklow Mountains. Today it gives rounded granite mountains such as Kippure, while the harder metamorphic rock forms peaks like Lugnaquilla.

Extrusive feature: the Antrim Plateau and the Giant's Causeway.
About 65 million years ago the Eurasian and North American plates were separating (a divergent boundary). Highly fluid basic lava rose through long cracks (fissure eruptions). The lava was low in gas, so eruptions were gentle and the lava spread over long distances. This went on and off for about 2 million years, building layer upon layer of basalt up to 1 km thick, forming a flat lava plateau over older chalk and limestone. Where the lava cooled quickly it contracted and cracked into hexagonal columns, forming the Giant's Causeway with over 40,000 columns. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a major tourist attraction.

prompt:
3B. Sedimentary Rocks
Examine the formation of sedimentary rocks, with reference to examples from Ireland.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediment that are compacted and cemented. Two Irish examples are limestone and sandstone.

Limestone (the Burren, Co. Clare; also the Central Lowlands):
Most Irish limestone formed about 350 million years ago when Ireland lay under a warm, shallow tropical sea. The shells and bones of sea creatures, rich in calcium carbonate, settled on the sea floor and mixed with fine mud, building up in layers (strata). Deposition was not continuous, so gaps called bedding planes formed between the layers. The weight of new layers squeezed the lower ones (compaction), pushing out water. Calcite carried by groundwater glued the grains together (cementation). Compaction and cementation together are called lithification. Later earth movements cracked the rock, forming vertical joints. Limestone is grey, layered, permeable and often contains fossils, showing it formed in the sea.

Sandstone (MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry - Old Red Sandstone):
Weathering broke older rocks into sand grains, mainly quartz. Rivers, wind or glaciers carried the grains and sorted them by size. When the agent lost energy, the grains settled in horizontal layers in deltas, deserts and lake beds. The layers built up and compacted the grains. Minerals such as silica, calcite or iron oxide from groundwater cemented them together, forming sandstone. Iron oxide gives it a red or rusty colour. It is rough, layered and porous.

prompt:
3C. Seismic Activity
Explain how the occurrence of earthquakes can be predicted and their effects reduced.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Prediction: monitoring seismic activity.
Earthquakes cannot be predicted exactly, but scientists monitor active areas closely. Seismometers in the ground detect vibrations and record them as seismograms; modern ones use three sensors to pinpoint location and size. Networks of seismometers, e.g. the US Geological Survey, give accurate readings in real time. Satellites detect ground shifts, cracks and deformation that show stress building up. In Japan the Japan Meteorological Agency monitors 24 hours a day.

Prediction: early warning systems.
These detect the first waves and send alerts seconds before shaking arrives. In Japan alerts go to mobile phones, trains and lifts stop automatically and gas lines shut off. Tsunami alerts give coastal people time to reach higher ground.

Reducing effects: earthquake-resistant buildings.
Base isolation uses flexible pads under a building so it sways gently, separate from the ground shaking. Dampers absorb vibrations, e.g. the Yokohama Landmark Tower. Reinforced concrete, steel frames and wood bend without breaking. Simple, symmetrical shapes spread seismic energy evenly.

Reducing effects: preparation.
Drills such as 'Drop, Cover and Hold On' are practised in Japanese schools and workplaces. Families keep emergency kits with food, water and first aid for three days and fix heavy furniture to walls.

In the 2024 Noto earthquake in Japan these measures limited deaths, but in Sulawesi in 2018, where sensors and sirens failed and building codes were ignored, over 4,300 people died.

prompt:
4B. Concept of a Region
Examine how culture or climate can be used to define regions, with reference to an example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
model_answer:
Climate can be used to define regions because climate is the average weather of a place over 30 years or more. Areas with similar temperature and rainfall form a climate region, and climate also decides the vegetation, soils, animals and farming in that region.

The Koppen classification, devised in 1884, uses temperature and precipitation to divide the world into five major climate regions: Tropical (A), Arid (B), Temperate (C), Continental (D) and Polar (E), with about 30 sub-zones.

Example 1: the hot desert region, e.g. the Sahara. It lies between 15 and 30 degrees north and south. It is defined by aridity: only 0 to 250 mm of rain a year, falling in short downpours. Temperatures range from 0 degrees C at night to 45 degrees C by day. Sinking air in high pressure blocks rain, and cold currents such as the Canaries Current make winds dry. These conditions give sparse vegetation such as cactus, and animals like camels.

Example 2: the cool temperate oceanic region, e.g. Ireland. It is Koppen type C with no dry season and warm summers. Winters average about 6 degrees C and summers about 16 degrees C. Rainfall is 800 to 2,000 mm spread through the year, brought by south-westerly winds and mid-latitude cyclones. The North Atlantic Drift keeps winters mild. This climate defines a region of deciduous woodland, brown earth soils and grass for pastoral farming.

A limitation is that climate regions have no sharp boundaries and the Koppen system ignores events such as storms and droughts.

Region: the West of Ireland, centred on Galway City. Secondary activity: medical device manufacturing, e.g. Boston Scientific at Ballybrit (since 1994, over 4,000 jobs, over 4 million devices exported a year) and Medtronic.

Factor 1: Government policy.
The Irish government uses tax policy to attract foreign direct investment. In 1997 corporation tax was cut to 12.5%, one of the lowest in the world; it is now 15% after the 2021 OECD agreement. This attracted US multinationals to set up factories in Ireland. IDA Ireland gives grants and business supports to high-tech manufacturers and promotes regional locations like Galway. EU membership is also a government policy advantage: firms in Galway get tariff-free access to a market of over 450 million people. Public investment, helped by EU structural funds, built the M6 motorway from Galway to Dublin, linking factories to Dublin Port and Airport. As a result Galway is called the medical device capital of Ireland.

Factor 2: Labour.
Galway has a highly skilled workforce. The University of Galway and Atlantic Technological University Galway produce graduates in engineering and life sciences. Because many MedTech firms cluster there, a large talent pool of engineers, scientists and technicians has built up, which attracts more firms. Galway has a large young population that is flexible and easy to train. Workers speak English, which makes communication with US management easier, and the city is culturally diverse, with multilingual skills useful for contact with plants in 40 countries. Boston Scientific has continued to expand in Galway, e.g. a EUR 100 million expansion in 2022 creating over 300 jobs.
