prompt:
Global Interdependence
We live in an interdependent global economy. Discuss the impact of social and political decisions with reference to each of the following:
- Economic and political refugees
- Migration patterns
- Human rights issues.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
We live in an interdependent world: decisions made by one government affect people thousands of kilometres away. This is clear when we look at refugees, migration patterns and human rights.

Aspect 1: Economic and political refugees.
A refugee is a person forced to flee their country because of persecution, conflict or violence. Political decisions such as going to war create refugees. Russia's decision to invade Ukraine in February 2022 caused one of the largest refugee crises in recent history: over 6.8 million refugees fled Ukraine, about 92% of them to Europe, and about 8 million more were displaced inside Ukraine. About 90% of those who left were women and children, because men aged 18-60 had to stay for military service. Other political decisions decided how these refugees were treated. Under the EU Temporary Protection scheme, Ireland gave Ukrainians housing, education and the right to work, and almost 120,000 have come to Ireland since 2022. In Sudan, the decision of two rival military groups to fight a civil war from April 2023 forced over 4 million people into overcrowded camps in neighbouring Chad and South Sudan. Economic refugees are created when climate change, poverty and debt make it impossible to earn a living. In the Sahel, drought and desertification have pushed displacement towards 5 million people. However, 'climate refugee' is not recognised under the 1951 Refugee Convention, so countries have no legal duty to accept them - a political decision with huge human consequences.

Aspect 2: Migration patterns.
Political decisions shape where people move. When Poland joined the EU in 2004, EU free movement meant young Poles could come to Ireland without a visa for higher wages. Over 1.2 billion euro was sent home to Poland in remittances in 2007 alone. Colonial history also shapes migration routes: after World War II, Britain invited over 500,000 people from the Caribbean and other Commonwealth countries between 1948 and 1971 (the Windrush generation) to rebuild the country. Today, government policy steers migration. Ireland's Critical Skills Employment Permit attracts highly skilled workers from outside the EEA to fill shortages in healthcare, engineering and IT. The EU Migration and Asylum Pact requires refugees to apply for asylum in the first EU country they enter. In 2024, Ireland had a net migration gain of 79,300 people, and migration is now the main driver of its population growth.

Aspect 3: Human rights issues.
Social and political decisions can protect or deny human rights. The Windrush Scandal showed how a political decision can harm people: many who had lived legally in Britain for decades had never received official papers, and some lost their jobs, were refused healthcare and were even deported. In Afghanistan, the Taliban closed girls' secondary schools and restricted women's university education and work; in 2023 about 3.7 million children were not in school. In Ireland, social attitudes have also affected migrants' rights: iReport.ie recorded 600 racism reports in 2022, and the 2024 Dublin riots were linked to fears about immigration. Positive decisions also exist: the Schools of Sanctuary programme makes schools safe and welcoming for refugees and asylum seekers, and Ireland's International Protection Bill (2025) aims to make the asylum system faster and fairer.

Conclusion: in an interdependent world, a decision to start a war, open a border or deny rights in one place changes the lives of millions of people in many other countries.

prompt:
Global Interdependence
Empowering people is a way of linking economic growth with human development.
Discuss this statement with reference to any three of the following:
- National debt
- Aid programmes
- Levels of exploitation at local and global scales
- Differing gender roles in society.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Economic growth means a country produces more wealth (higher GDP or GNI). Human development means people live longer, healthier, better-educated lives, as measured by the Human Development Index (HDI). Growth only becomes development when people are empowered to share in it.

Aspect 1: National debt.
When a country carries heavy debt, much of its money goes on repayments instead of schools and hospitals. After the 2008 crash, Ireland's debt reached 117% of GDP in 2012. Careful management cut it to 34.9% of GDP by 2025. This freed money for services that empower people, such as the new National Children's Hospital in Dublin, new schools in fast-growing areas like west Dublin and Cork, SUSI student grants and free schoolbooks. Ireland's HDI is now 0.949, among the highest in the world. In contrast, Afghanistan cannot borrow because lenders see it as too risky. With little money, education and healthcare are underfunded and up to 97% of Afghans live in poverty; its HDI is only 0.462. Debt can also be used to control: China's Belt and Road Initiative lends money for ports and railways, but critics say it can trap poorer countries in debt. Managing debt well allows growth to be turned into human development.

Aspect 2: Aid programmes.
Good aid empowers people to help themselves rather than creating dependency. Irish Aid works in partnership with local communities, following its 'A Better World' policy of 'reaching the furthest behind first'. In Ethiopia, the top recipient of Irish bilateral aid in 2024, women are given training, credit and livestock to set up small businesses, giving them income and independence. Farmers are supported with drought-resistant crops such as potatoes and with agroforestry; in Tigray, water tanks, irrigation channels and small dams helped some farmers increase harvests by up to 30% even in low rainfall. Training nurses and midwives raised births with a midwife present from 18% to 28% between 2020 and 2025, and infant mortality fell. School feeding programmes give children the energy to learn. By educating teachers and local leaders, Irish Aid makes sure programmes continue after it leaves. This links growth in farm output and incomes with better health and education.

Aspect 3: Differing gender roles in society.
When women are empowered, both the economy and human development improve. In Ireland, the Marriage Bar forced women to leave many jobs when they married until 1973. Its removal, equal pay laws from 1975 and more education meant women now make up about 47% of the workforce and over half of third-level students. This boosted growth and led to smaller families. In India, Kerala shows the link clearly: with female literacy of 97%, it has a fertility rate of 1.7 and one of the highest life expectancies in India. In Bihar, where female literacy can be as low as 60% and early marriage is common, the fertility rate is 3.0 and poverty is higher. India's 'Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao' campaign promotes girls' education. In Afghanistan, Taliban policies that bar girls from secondary school hold back both growth and development. The Gender Development Index (GDI) and UN Sustainable Development Goal 5 measure and promote this equality.

Conclusion: economic growth alone does not guarantee a better life. Reducing debt to fund services, giving aid that builds people's own skills and treating women equally all empower people, turning growth into real human development.

prompt:
Global Interdependence
Examine sustainable development as a model for future development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Sustainable development aims to improve quality of life by solving today's problems, such as hunger, poverty and pollution, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It has three interconnected pillars: environmental, economic and social. The UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set worldwide targets, including ending poverty, fighting climate change and ensuring clean water and good health for everyone.

Aspect 1: The environmental pillar.
Older models of development often damaged the environment. Under modernisation, China moved from a rural, agricultural country to an industrial superpower and lifted many out of poverty, but rapid city growth caused overcrowding and pollution. In Beijing the number of cars rose from 77,000 in 1978 to millions by 2018. Sustainable development protects clean air, water and forests. Finland, ranked first on the 2025 SDG Index, prioritises recycling and clean transport and aims to be carbon neutral by 2035 by cutting emissions and strengthening carbon sinks. In Ireland, Bord na Mona's peatland rehabilitation stores carbon, improves water quality and reduces flooding. The Crumlin Village scheme in Dublin uses nature-based drainage (SuDS) such as tree pits and filter drains, reducing flooding and pollution while adding green space. Under the Paris Agreement, 196 countries agreed to keep warming well below 2 degrees C, with net zero as the overall aim.

Aspect 2: The economic pillar.
Sustainable development needs a stable economy with jobs and businesses, but growth must not destroy the resources it depends on. Iceland shows this: geothermal energy gives cheap electricity to about 90% of homes, supports aluminium smelting and greenhouses, and cuts imported fuel, while lowering CO2 emissions by up to 37%. Ireland's Carbon Farming Scheme pays farmers to store carbon in their soil, and Food Vision 2030 aims to make Ireland a leader in sustainable food. In fishing, EU Total Allowable Catches and Maximum Sustainable Yield rules let fishers earn a living while preventing fish stocks from collapsing. By contrast, protectionism (such as US tariffs) may protect jobs in the short term, but leads to trade wars and higher prices.

Aspect 3: The social pillar.
Development must be fair and meet everyone's needs. Finland balances growth with strong health and education. In Ireland, the National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040) is built on National Strategic Outcomes based on the SDGs, including compact growth, sustainable mobility and access to quality childcare, education and health services. It aims for 50% of new city homes to be built on brownfield and derelict sites, and for new developments to be built around public transport, such as Clonburris in South Dublin. Rural plans support community hubs such as GTEIC in Donegal, giving remote workers broadband and social connection. Irish Aid supports the SDGs abroad, for example by improving maternal health and girls' opportunities in Ethiopia.

Aspect 4: Challenges of the model.
Sustainable development balances nature, people and money, but it takes time and is harder to put into practice than simpler models. The pillars can conflict: cutting Irish herd sizes helps the climate but threatens farm incomes. Powerful leaders can also slow progress: the US withdrew from the Paris Agreement in January 2025.

Conclusion: although slower and harder to achieve, sustainable development is the best model for the future because it is the only one that protects the planet, the economy and people together.

prompt:
Geoecology
Examine how any three of the following processes impact on soil characteristics:
- Weathering
- Podzolisation
- Calcification
- Soil erosion.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Soil characteristics include colour, texture, structure, drainage, pH (acidity) and fertility. Different processes change these characteristics.

Aspect 1: Weathering.
Weathering breaks down rocks into smaller pieces at the Earth's surface, and these pieces become the mineral matter in soil. The type of parent rock decides many soil characteristics. Physical weathering such as freeze-thaw action breaks rock into angular fragments without changing its minerals, giving coarse, stony soils on upland slopes such as Croagh Patrick. Chemical weathering changes the minerals. Carbonation dissolves limestone, and oxidation turns iron in sandstone into reddish iron oxide, which gives soils a red or rusty colour, as in the MacGillycuddy's Reeks. Granite in west Galway weathers into poor clay soils that are unsuitable for tillage. In the east and south of Ireland, soils developed on a mix of weathered glacial deposits about 10,000 years old. These contain a variety of minerals and have a loamy texture (a balance of sand, silt and clay). Combined with mild temperatures, this gives fertile, well-drained brown earth soils, the most common soil in Ireland.

Aspect 2: Podzolisation.
Podzolisation happens in areas of heavy rainfall, often under coniferous forest. Heavy rain moves down through the soil and washes nutrients from the topsoil into lower horizons. This is leaching. Conifer needles produce poor plant litter and make the soil acidic, so there is little microbial action and the humus is a raw acid humus. Leaching leaves an ash-grey layer near the top of the soil. Lower down, iron and organic matter build up and harden into an iron pan (hardpan). Below this is a reddish-brown layer, then the parent material. The iron pan stops water draining, so podzols are poorly drained and easily waterlogged. As a result, podzols are infertile, acidic soils with a clear layered profile. Examples are found in Counties Cork and Cavan, and in east Mayo, hardpans around Ballyhaunis cause waterlogging and low crop yields.

Aspect 3: Soil erosion.
Soil erosion is the removal of the top layer of soil by water or wind. It strips away the most fertile part of the soil: the humus and nutrients in the topsoil. In Malawi, drought dries and loosens the soil, and when heavy rain follows, mudslides, landslides and soil erosion destroy crops and strip nutrients from the land. Cyclone Freddy in 2023 flooded thousands of hectares of farmland. In Afghanistan, soil erosion and desertification have lowered farm output; in the north, loss of grassland and failed harvests mean families lose livestock and income. Even in Ireland, heavy rain causes waterlogging, soil erosion and the runoff of nutrients and pesticides into rivers. When soil is eroded, what remains is thinner, less fertile and holds less water, so crop yields fall.

Aspect 4: Comparison of the effects.
These processes produce very different soils. Brown earths, formed under deciduous forest with low rainfall and little leaching, are dark, rich in humus, well-drained and fertile, ideal for arable farming. Podzols, formed by heavy leaching, are acidic, layered and infertile. Eroded soils lose their fertile topsoil altogether.

Conclusion: weathering provides the raw mineral matter of soil, podzolisation reorganises nutrients and iron within the profile, and soil erosion removes the soil entirely. Each process changes soil colour, structure, drainage and fertility, which in turn affects farming.

prompt:
Geoecology
Examine the influence of mineral matter, air, water and organic matter on soil development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Soil is made up of four parts: mineral matter, air, water and organic matter. The balance between them decides how a soil develops and how fertile it is.

Aspect 1: Mineral matter.
Mineral matter comes from the weathering of parent rock and from deposits such as glacial till. It makes up most of a soil and decides its texture and many of its nutrients. In the east and south of Ireland, brown earth soils developed on glacial deposits about 10,000 years old. These deposits contain a variety of minerals and give a loamy texture - a balance of sand, silt and clay - with a granular structure of rounded, grain-like particles. This makes the soil well-drained, well-aerated and fertile. In contrast, granite in west Galway weathers into poor clay soils that are unsuitable for tillage. Soils over impermeable bedrock with a high clay content drain badly, which leads to gley soils. Iron in the parent material also affects colour: oxidation gives reddish soils, while in waterlogged soils iron turns bluish-grey.

Aspect 2: Air.
Air fills the pore spaces between soil particles. Aeration (the amount of air in soil) is needed by plant roots and by the microorganisms, earthworms and insects that break down organic matter. Well-aerated brown earths support high biological activity all year because the ground rarely freezes. When soil is waterlogged, air is pushed out. In gley soils, microorganisms use up the oxygen while decomposing organic matter. This is called anaerobic reduction. Chemical reactions then turn the iron a bluish-grey colour. Poor aeration also gives gleys a blocky structure of cube-shaped particles, which restricts roots and limits oxygen for plants. Gley soils are found in Cavan, Monaghan, Leitrim and Clare, and are only moderately fertile.

Aspect 3: Water.
Water carries nutrients to plants, but too much or too little changes soil development. Rainfall in Ireland ranges from about 800 mm in the east to 1,600 mm in the west. In the drier east, little leaching occurs, so nutrients stay in the topsoil and brown earths are well-drained and fertile. In wetter areas, water percolating down washes nutrients into lower horizons (leaching). Under heavy rain and coniferous forest this forms podzols, with an ash-grey leached layer and an iron pan that blocks drainage. Where drainage is poor and the ground is waterlogged for long periods, peat soils develop. These are over 90% water, which keeps bogs wet and preserves dead plant matter.

Aspect 4: Organic matter.
Organic matter comes from dead plants and animals. Broken down by microbes, earthworms, millipedes and beetles, it becomes humus, a dark, jelly-like substance that holds water and nutrients. Ireland's deciduous trees, such as oak and ash, shed their leaves each autumn, and the mild climate lets decomposers recycle this leaf litter for most of the year. This gives brown earths their high humus content and dark colour. Earthworms mix organic and mineral matter, so there are no sharp layers. Badgers digging setts also mix the soil and add nutrients. Where decomposition is slow, organic matter builds up instead. In waterlogged, acidic conditions, mosses such as sphagnum build up faster than they decay, forming peat. Under conifers, needles give poor litter and a raw acid humus.

Conclusion: the four parts work together. A good balance of minerals, air, water and humus produces fertile brown earths, while too much water and too little air produce gleys, podzols and peat.

prompt:
Geoecology
Biomes are altered by human activity. Examine this statement with reference to each of the following activities:
- The felling of tropical rainforests
- Intensive agricultural practices
- Industrial development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
A biome is a large, distinct natural region with a particular climate, plants, animals and soils. Human activity can change biomes greatly.

Aspect 1: The felling of tropical rainforests.
Tropical rainforests, such as those in Brazil, have a hot, wet climate with 2,000 to 10,000 mm of rain a year. This supports lush vegetation, rapid growth and very diverse animals, birds and insects, such as the toucan. The forest helps to make its own rain: about half of the convectional rain comes from plants, through transpiration. Each tree releases on average 755 litres of water a year, which rises, condenses and falls as rain. When trees are felled, this moisture is lost, so less rain falls and the climate of the region becomes drier. Habitats are destroyed, so many plants and animals lose their homes and biodiversity falls. Deforestation also releases carbon dioxide and removes trees that absorb it, adding to global warming, which further changes biomes around the world.

Aspect 2: Intensive agricultural practices.
Ireland's natural biome is a temperate deciduous rainforest of oak, ash, alder, birch and hazel. Centuries of clearance for farming have taken Ireland from one of the most forested to one of the least forested countries in Europe: only 10% of Ireland is woodland, and only one-fifth of that is native. Modern intensive dairy and beef farming adds further damage. Nitrates and phosphates from slurry and fertilisers run off into streams, rivers and lakes and pollute them. Livestock give off methane and fertilisers release nitrous oxide, both greenhouse gases. Pesticides and the loss of hedgerows harm pollinators: 30% of Ireland's 100 native bee species are at risk of extinction. In 2025 the European Environment Agency said 85% of Ireland's protected habitats were in an 'unfavourable' state. Schemes such as ACRES and organic farming now try to reverse this, for example by using natural pest control such as ladybirds.

Aspect 3: Industrial development (and urban growth).
Industry and the cities that grow around it take over natural land. Around Dublin, urban sprawl has spread housing, factories and retail parks onto farmland in Meath and Kildare. Woodland, hedgerows and wetlands are destroyed, harming red squirrels, pine martens, hares and badgers, and pollinators lose their food. Waste, pollution and car emissions rise; urban foxes now scavenge bins and have shorter lives. Along Spain's Mediterranean coast, development for the tourism industry has doubled the built-up area, destroying coastal ecosystems. Boats and cruise ships anchoring off the coast damage Posidonia seagrass meadows, which produce oxygen, provide habitats, prevent coastal erosion and store carbon. Industrial emissions are also the main cause of climate change, which melts permafrost, raises sea levels and threatens coastal habitats such as dunes and salt marshes.

Aspect 4: Responses.
Humans can also help biomes recover. Reafforestation and the restoration of wetlands and peatlands store carbon and improve biodiversity. In Spain, tourism taxes fund over 5 million euro a year of coastal habitat restoration, and Posidonia clean-ups involve tens of thousands of people. In Dublin, projects such as Bridgefoot Street Park have planted over 180 trees.

Conclusion: felling forests, farming intensively and developing industry all change the plants, animals, soils and even climate of biomes, so careful, sustainable management is needed to protect them.

prompt:
Culture and Identity
Examine the importance of religion as a cultural indicator.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
A cultural indicator is a feature, such as language or religion, that helps to identify a cultural group. Religion is one of the most important cultural indicators because it shapes people's values, family life, landscapes and even the borders of countries.

Aspect 1: Religion shapes family life and population.
Religion influences how many children people have. In Ireland, the Catholic Church strongly influenced society and was closely aligned with the State. It encouraged large families, and contraception was not easily available until 1985. In 1961 the fertility rate was 3.78 children per woman, and families of over four children were common. As the Church's influence weakened - its special status was removed in 1973 - families became smaller, and the fertility rate fell to 1.5 by 2024. In northern Indian states such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, traditional Hindu values favour large families, early marriage and 'son preference', because sons carry the family name and daughters need a dowry. This keeps birth rates high and affects the balance of boys and girls. So religion is a clear indicator of a group's values and family patterns.

Aspect 2: Religion and political boundaries and conflict.
Religion can define nations. In 1947 Britain divided 'British India' along religious lines into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan. Millions moved across the new borders: about 12 million fled Pakistan for India and over 10 million went the other way, and about 1 million people died in violence. Religion continues to fuel the Kashmir dispute. Kashmir's ruler chose to join India, although 80% of its people were Muslims who wanted to join Pakistan. Wars followed in 1947-48, 1965 and 1999, and attacks continue, such as at Pahalgam in 2025. In 2019, India split the region into Jammu and Kashmir (Muslim-majority Kashmir and Hindu-majority Jammu) and Buddhist-majority Ladakh, which caused outrage in Kashmir and Pakistan. In the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Catholic nationalist communities suffered higher unemployment and lower wages.

Aspect 3: Religion in the landscape.
Religion leaves visible marks that identify a culture. In Ireland, many placenames come from religious sites: cill and eaglais mean church (Cill Dara, Kildare, 'Dara's Church'), mainistir means monastery (Monasterboice) and tearmann means sanctuary (Termon). Medieval Galway gained a religious function with St Nicholas' Church (1320) and the arrival of the Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits. Early Christian monasteries such as Clonmacnoise and Glendalough are now major tourist attractions. In India, the Golden Temple of Amritsar is the Sikh religion's most important pilgrimage site.

Aspect 4: Religion and migration.
Migration brings new religions and makes societies more diverse. In Ireland, Catholicism is strongest among older rural people, while migration has brought Islam, Hinduism and Orthodox Christianity, mainly to the cities. Migrants often choose countries with a similar religion and culture; Irish emigrants to Britain, the US and Australia shared Christian traditions, which made settling easier.

Conclusion: religion is a powerful cultural indicator. It shapes family size, defines national borders, marks the landscape with churches and placenames, and changes as people migrate.

prompt:
Culture and Identity
Examine how different cultural groups can exist within nation states, with reference to example(s) you have studied.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
A nation state is a country whose people are often seen as sharing one culture. In reality, most states contain several cultural groups that differ in language, religion or ethnicity. They can live together peacefully, or tension and conflict can arise.

Aspect 1: Language groups within a state - Ireland and India.
In Ireland, Irish speakers form a distinct cultural group in Gaeltacht areas of Galway, Kerry and Donegal. Planning policy protects them: in the Galway County Development Plan, planning permission in the Gaeltacht is given to people who can prove they speak Irish, to protect the language and culture. Udaras na Gaeltachta supports Gaeltacht businesses, and the GTEIC hub in An Tearmann, Co. Donegal gives remote workers jobs so young people can stay. However, a lack of jobs in the past led young people to leave places like Connemara and Ballyferriter. India is a much larger example: Hindi speakers are concentrated in the north and Tamil speakers in the south, while big cities like Mumbai and Delhi are mixed. These groups co-exist within one federal state.

Aspect 2: Religious and ethnic groups - India's tensions.
India contains Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Buddhists and many ethnic groups. Sometimes they clash. In Kashmir, where 60% of people in the Indian-controlled part are Muslim and many want to join Pakistan, there have been wars and repeated attacks. In 2019, India divided the region into Jammu and Kashmir (Muslim-majority Kashmir and Hindu-majority Jammu) and Buddhist-majority Ladakh, which caused outrage. In north-east India, ethnic violence and separatist movements continue: in Manipur in 2024, 70 people were killed and 60,000 left their homes. These examples show that cultural groups within a state can face tension when they feel their identity is under threat.

Aspect 3: Migrant communities - multicultural Ireland.
Migration has created many new cultural groups in Ireland. Polish, Brazilian, Ukrainian and Nigerian communities now live throughout the country. In Dublin, over 17% of residents are non-Irish nationals, from countries such as Brazil, India, Romania, Poland and Nigeria. They bring new languages, food, religions, shops and festivals. Schools provide English as an Additional Language (EAL) classes, the Schools of Sanctuary programme welcomes refugees, and Failte Isteach volunteers help immigrants practise English, building friendship and trust. However, tension can also occur: there were 600 racism reports in 2022, and anti-immigration feeling was linked to the 2024 Dublin riots.

Aspect 4: Former colonial groups - the Windrush generation in Britain.
Between 1948 and 1971, over 500,000 people from the Caribbean and other Commonwealth countries came to Britain to help rebuild it after World War II. They worked on buses, in factories and in the new NHS, and formed a distinct Caribbean community. They faced racism, poor housing and social exclusion, and in the Windrush Scandal some were even deported because they lacked official papers. Today they are an established part of British society.

Conclusion: different cultural groups can co-exist within nation states when their rights, language and religion are protected and they are welcomed and included. Where groups feel threatened or excluded, tension and even conflict can follow.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Describe the formation of each of the following and discuss its impact on weather patterns:
- Mid-latitude depressions
- Anticyclones
- Land and sea breezes.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1: Mid-latitude depressions.
Formation: mid-latitude depressions (frontal depressions or cyclones) form between about 30 and 60 degrees latitude. They form at the polar front, where cold, dense polar air from the north meets warm, less dense tropical air from the south. A disturbance, often caused by the jet stream, makes a wave or kink in the front, and an area of low pressure forms at its tip. As the low deepens, air circulates around it. Because of the Coriolis Effect, it spins anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere. Warm air pushes forward at the warm front and rises slowly over the cold air. Behind it, cold air moves faster and undercuts the warm air at the cold front. Eventually the cold front catches up with the warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground to form an occluded front. The depression then weakens and dies away.
Impact on weather: depressions bring unsettled, windy and wet weather. At the warm front, layered clouds (cirrus, altostratus, nimbostratus) bring steady drizzle and persistent rain. At the cold front, towering cumulonimbus clouds bring heavy showers and sometimes thunderstorms, followed by a sharp drop in temperature and a change in wind direction. Ireland gets about five a year, carried by the prevailing south-westerly winds. Strong depressions cause damaging gusts and storm surges. Storm Eowyn (January 2025) had a record gust of 184 km/h at Mace Head, Co. Galway, and caused widespread power cuts.

Aspect 2: Anticyclones.
Formation: an anticyclone is a large area of high pressure caused by sinking air. Cold, heavy air descends from high altitude and spreads outwards from the centre. The Coriolis Effect makes it circulate slowly clockwise in the northern hemisphere. As the air sinks, it is compressed and warms, which stops clouds forming. Isobars are far apart, so winds are light.
Impact on weather: anticyclones bring settled, calm, dry and clear weather. In summer they give sunny days, heatwaves and sometimes drought; for example, 33 degrees C was recorded in the Phoenix Park, Dublin on 18 July 2022. In winter, clear skies let heat escape at night, giving frost, fog and very cold conditions. When high pressure sits to the north of Ireland, it can draw in cold air from Siberia: in 2018, 'the Beast from the East' brought snow and temperatures as low as -18 degrees C. Anticyclones can also 'block' depressions, forcing them to track around and keeping weather settled for days or weeks.

Aspect 3: Land and sea breezes.
Formation: land and sea breezes form because land and sea heat up and cool down at different speeds. Land heats and cools quickly, while the sea heats and cools slowly and holds its heat for longer. During a sunny day, the land warms faster than the sea. Air over the land is heated, expands and rises, creating lower pressure over the land. Cooler air over the sea, at higher pressure, flows in towards the land to replace it. This is a sea breeze. At night the land cools quickly, while the sea stays warmer. Now air rises over the sea, and cooler air flows from the land out to sea. This is a land breeze.
Impact on weather: sea breezes bring cooler, fresher air to the coast on hot summer days, so coastal temperatures are lower than inland. The rising air over the land can form cumulus clouds and sometimes showers inland in the afternoon. Land breezes are usually gentler and blow offshore at night and in the early morning. These breezes are strongest in calm, sunny weather, often during an anticyclone, when there is a big difference between land and sea temperatures.

Conclusion: depressions, anticyclones and land and sea breezes all form through differences in air pressure and temperature, and they explain much of the day-to-day change in Ireland's weather.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Give an account of how atmosphere-ocean phenomena (e.g. pressure, temperature, wind and humidity) are measured and examine the importance of such measurements.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1: Measuring pressure and temperature.
Atmospheric pressure is measured with a barometer, in millibars (mb) or hectopascals (hPa). Inside, a flexible metal box expands or contracts as pressure changes, moving a pointer on a dial. Meteorologists join places of equal pressure with isobars on synoptic charts, drawn at 4 hPa intervals. Low pressure (L) shows a depression and high pressure (H) an anticyclone. Temperature is measured with a maximum-minimum thermometer, in degrees Celsius. It contains alcohol and mercury, and small metal pieces in the tubes mark the highest and lowest temperatures reached. Lines of equal temperature are called isotherms. These measurements matter because falling pressure warns that a depression is approaching, bringing wind and rain, while rising pressure shows settled weather is coming. Temperature records show heatwaves and cold snaps, such as 33 degrees C in the Phoenix Park in July 2022 and -17.5 degrees C at Straide, Co. Mayo in December 2010.

Aspect 2: Measuring wind and humidity.
Wind speed is measured with an anemometer, in kilometres per hour. Three cups rotate faster as the wind gets stronger, and a meter counts the rotations. Wind direction is shown by a wind vane, whose arrow points to the direction the wind blows from. Wind data is shown on wind roses and wind barb charts. Relative humidity is measured with a hygrometer, as a percentage, where saturated air is 100%. It has a dry bulb and a wet bulb thermometer, the wet bulb kept moist with muslin dipped in water. Humidity is worked out from the difference between the two temperatures. Rainfall is measured in millimetres with a rain gauge, and cloud cover in oktas (eighths of the sky) using a ceilometer. These measurements are vital for warnings: during Storm Eowyn in January 2025, gusts of 184 km/h were recorded at Mace Head, Co. Galway, and Met Eireann issued a status red warning in advance.

Aspect 3: Remote sensing of the atmosphere and oceans.
Modern technology measures conditions far above the ground and across the oceans. Weather balloons (radiosondes) measure temperature, humidity and pressure at different heights and send back the data. Doppler radar detects rain and wind speed and direction, including wind shear. Satellites give global coverage: the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite loops the world every 100 minutes, and Copernicus satellites monitor gases in the atmosphere, ice-sheet melting and sea levels. Weather stations, buoys and research vessels collect data at sea. In Indonesia, tsunami warning buoys measure changes in the ocean, though in 2018 many sensors were not working. In Dublin, 14 sensors on the River Liffey give real-time water level and flow data.

Aspect 4: The importance of these measurements.
Accurate measurements allow weather forecasting. Met Eireann collects data, finds patterns and produces synoptic charts. Warnings save lives and property by giving people time to prepare for storms, floods and snow. Early warning systems such as the European Flood Awareness System (EFAS) and the European Forest Fire Information System help emergency services act quickly. Farmers use forecasts to plan harvests and protect livestock. Long-term measurements are essential for tracking climate change: records show that global temperatures rose 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels for the first time in 2024, and Ireland's temperature anomaly graph shows clear warming since 1990. Data on the AMOC shows it is at its weakest in about 1,600 years. Under the Paris Agreement, every country must monitor and report emissions.

Conclusion: from simple barometers to satellites, measuring the atmosphere and oceans lets us forecast weather, warn people of danger and understand how our climate is changing.

prompt:
The Atmosphere - Ocean Environment
Examine how climate characteristics influence economic development.
(80 marks)
model_answer:
Climate is the average weather of a region over 30 years or more. Its temperature, rainfall and sunshine strongly influence which economic activities can develop and how wealthy a region becomes.

Aspect 1: Climate and agriculture in Ireland.
Ireland has a cool temperate oceanic climate, with mild winters of about 5-6 degrees C, summers of 15-16 degrees C and rain all year. This is ideal for growing grass, so Irish farming is dominated by beef and dairy. Agriculture is worth 8% of GDP, a record 17 billion euro in 2024, and Ireland produced 603,000 tonnes of beef in 2024, 90% of it exported. But climate also creates regional differences. The mountainous west gets about 1,600 mm of rain a year, almost twice the east's 800 mm, which is in a rain shadow. Heavy rain in the west causes leaching and waterlogging, limiting crops, so farms are smaller and less profitable; less than 2% of Irish cereal was grown in the West in 2023. The drier, sunnier east has a growing season of 280 days, over a month longer, so it supports commercial tillage farming. Climate therefore helps explain why the east is wealthier than the west.

Aspect 2: Climate and tourism in Spain.
Spain's Mediterranean climate has long, hot, dry summers of about 28 degrees C in July and over 300 days of sunshine. This dependable 'sun and sea' climate attracts northern Europeans from cooler, wetter countries. Mass tourism grew from fewer than 1 million visitors in 1950 to a record 94 million in 2024. Tourism employs nearly 3 million people and is worth 15% of Spain's GDP. Mild winters of 15-18 degrees C now attract visitors outside the summer, creating more year-round jobs. Fishing villages such as Torremolinos became busy resorts. However, climate change brings heatwaves of 35-40 degrees C and drought, which may reduce summer demand and strain water supplies.

Aspect 3: Dry climates and extreme events limit development.
Harsh climates can hold back development. Afghanistan has a dry climate with frequent droughts and extreme temperature ranges, and has suffered severe drought since 2021. About 80% of Afghans depend on farming, so drought means failed crops, food shortages and malnutrition, and up to 97% of Afghans live in poverty. In Malawi, a sub-tropical climate with a rainy season and a dry season makes farmers vulnerable when rains come late. Cyclone Freddy in 2023 wiped out the crops and livestock of over 2 million farmers, and maize production fell by 11.4% between 2023 and 2024. This causes higher food prices, unemployment and lost export earnings. Even Ireland suffers: Storm Eowyn in 2025 caused power outages and costly repairs.

Aspect 4: Climate as an energy resource.
Climate can also provide resources. Ireland's strong prevailing south-westerly winds are used for wind energy, which rose from 7% of Ireland's electricity in 2012 to 20% in 2022, reducing the need for imported fossil fuels. In polar and sub-polar regions, by contrast, extreme cold, short growing seasons and permafrost limit farming and settlement, so economic activity is sparse.

Conclusion: climate influences economic development in many ways. A favourable climate supports profitable farming, tourism and renewable energy, while drought, extreme cold and storms hold back development and keep many people in poverty.
